explanation: First derive each molecular formula from the skeletal drawing (line ends and vertices are carbons with implicit H; heteroatoms are labelled): I = butan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH = C4H10O; II = butanal, CH3CH2CH2CHO = C4H8O; III = 2-methoxypropane, (CH3)2CH-O-CH3 = C4H10O; IV = butanal drawn with the C=O on the left = C4H8O; V = pentan-1-ol = C5H12O. Isomers require identical formula AND different connectivity. A (I & III) is correct: both are C4H10O, but I is a primary alcohol and III is an ether, so their atoms are connected differently — genuine constitutional isomers. B (II & IV) is the key trap: they share the formula C4H8O and are drawn differently, but tracing the bonds shows both are CH3CH2CH2CHO — the SAME compound (butanal) merely re-oriented, so they are identical, not isomers; this catches students who equate 'same formula + looks different' with isomerism while ignoring connectivity. C (I & II) traps those who compare only the carbon skeleton (both are four-carbon chains) without counting hydrogens: the C=O in II removes two H, giving C4H8O ≠ C4H10O, so the formulas differ. D (I & V) traps 'same functional group ⇒ isomers': both are straight-chain primary alcohols, but they differ by one CH2 (C4H10O vs C5H12O) — they are homologues, not isomers. E (III & V) traps 'both contain oxygen ⇒ isomers': their formulas (C4H10O vs C5H12O) are different, so they cannot be isomers.

stem: During the analysis of a volatile compound isolated from a plant essential oil, high-resolution mass spectrometry establishes its molecular formula as C6H10. Before any spectroscopic data on bond types are available, which single statement about the compound's structure is necessarily correct on the basis of the formula alone?
choices: Its carbon skeleton must be acyclic (open-chain), because only multiple bonds — not rings — reduce the hydrogen count below that of the saturated alkane.

It possesses two degrees of unsaturation, which may be realized as any combination of rings and carbon–carbon π bonds (e.g. one triple bond, two double bonds, one ring plus one double bond, or two rings).
It must contain exactly one carbon–carbon triple bond and no ring, since a triple bond is the only way to account for the missing hydrogens.
It could be an aromatic (benzene-type) compound, because a six-carbon ring is compatible with this molecular formula.
It has four degrees of unsaturation, equal to the number of hydrogen atoms missing relative to the corresponding saturated alkane C6H14.
explanation: The saturated (acyclic, all-single-bond) alkane with 6 carbons is C6H14. The compound C6H10 is missing 4 hydrogen atoms; degree of unsaturation (index of hydrogen deficiency) = (missing H)/2 = 4/2 = 2, or directly DoU = (2·6 + 2 − 10)/2 = 2. Each degree of unsaturation corresponds to either one ring OR one π bond, so the two degrees may be distributed in several structurally distinct ways — this is exactly what B states, making it the only claim guaranteed by the formula alone. Distractor A encodes the misconception that only multiple bonds lower the hydrogen count, forgetting that each ring also removes 2 H and counts as one degree of unsaturation. Distractor C assumes the deficiency must be a single triple bond; a triple bond does supply 2 degrees, but it is only one of several possibilities, so it is not necessary. Distractor D reflects the trap of equating any unsaturated six-carbon ring with benzene: an aromatic benzene ring carries 4 degrees of unsaturation (3 π bonds + 1 ring), so an aromatic compound would need DoU ≥ 4 and cannot have formula C6H10 (benzene itself is C6H6). Distractor E is the classic arithmetic error of reporting the number of missing hydrogens (4) as the degree of unsaturation, omitting the division by 2.

stem: Propan-1-ol has the condensed structure CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. A constitutional (structural) isomer must share the same molecular formula but differ in how the atoms are connected. Which of the following compounds is a constitutional isomer of propan-1-ol?
explanation: First determine the molecular formula of the target: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH = C₃H₈O. A constitutional isomer must match C₃H₈O exactly yet connect the atoms differently. A) Methoxyethane, CH₃–O–CH₂CH₃, counts to C₃H₈O and routes the same atoms into an ether linkage instead of an alcohol — a genuine functional-group (constitutional) isomer. Correct. B) Propanal is C₃H₆O (two fewer H); it is the oxidation product, not an isomer — trap for students who assume a carbonyl compound with the same carbon count is automatically an isomer. C) Propane is C₃H₈ (no oxygen); it shares the carbon skeleton but drops the O — trap for students who match only the carbon backbone and ignore heteroatoms. D) Propane-1,2-diol is C₃H₈O₂ (an extra O); still an alcohol with three carbons, so it looks like an "alcohol isomer," but adding a second –OH changes the formula. E) Butan-1-ol is C₄H₁₀O — the next homolog up; a member of the same series is not an isomer because it has a different molecular formula. Only A satisfies both requirements: identical formula, different connectivity.

stem: A student adds a small, equal sample of each of the five compounds A–E (skeletal structures shown) to separate test tubes, each containing aqueous sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO₃). In only one tube does a steady stream of gas bubbles (CO₂) form. Reading the skeletal formulas carefully, which compound is responsible for the effervescence?
explanation:
Only a carboxylic acid (–COOH) is acidic enough to react with sodium hydrogen carbonate and release CO₂ gas. The task is therefore twofold: read each skeletal structure correctly, then recall which functional group reacts with bicarbonate.

Correct — C: propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂–C(=O)–OH. The carbonyl carbon carries a double-bonded O (drawn up) AND a single-bonded –OH (drawn to the side): this is the carboxyl group. It is the only structure whose oxygen bears an acidic O–H, so it alone liberates CO₂.

A (trap: carbonyl ≠ carboxyl): butan-2-one, a ketone with C=O on an internal carbon bonded to two other carbons. It has a carbonyl but no acidic O–H, so it is unreactive toward NaHCO₃. Students who equate any C=O with acidity fall here.

B (trap: ester looks like an acid): methyl propanoate, –C(=O)–O–CH₃. It shows both a double-bonded O and a single-bonded O, so the –C(=O)O– motif superficially resembles a carboxyl. But the second oxygen carries a carbon (a methyl group), not an acidic H, making it a neutral ester that does not react. This is the key discriminator from C, where that oxygen is –OH.

D (trap: any O–H must be acidic): butan-1-ol, an alcohol. It does have an O–H, but alcohols are far too weakly acidic to protonate bicarbonate, so no CO₂ is evolved.

E (trap: aldehyde ≈ acid): butanal, an aldehyde with a terminal C=O (and an implied H on that carbon). It can be oxidised to an acid and has a C=O plus a hydrogen, but that H sits on carbon, not oxygen; there is no –COOH, so it does not react with NaHCO₃.

Thus the reasoning requires distinguishing –COOH from ketone (A), ester (B), alcohol (D), and aldehyde (E), all of which share a visual feature with the carboxyl group.

stem:
Copper metal dissolves in dilute nitric acid according to the balanced equation:

3 Cu(s) + 8 HNO₃(aq) → 3 Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2 NO(g) + 4 H₂O(l)

Note that of the eight nitrogen atoms from HNO₃, six end up as nitrate ions in Cu(NO₃)₂ and two end up in NO. In this reaction, which species acts as the reducing agent?
explanation:
The reducing agent is the reactant that is itself oxidized (loses electrons). Copper goes from 0 in Cu(s) to +2 in Cu(NO₃)₂, losing 2 electrons per atom — it is oxidized, so Cu is the reducing agent (C, correct).

A) HNO₃ is the classic reversal trap: its nitrogen IS reduced (+5 in HNO₃ → +2 in NO), so it gains electrons and is therefore the OXIDIZING agent, not the reducing agent. Students who swap the two definitions pick this.

B) NO is the reduction PRODUCT. Its nitrogen (+2) did change oxidation state, tempting students who track "which element changed," but an agent must be a reactant that donates/accepts electrons — NO is what remains after reduction, not the species doing the reducing. It has already been reduced, so it cannot be the reducing agent.

D) The NO₃⁻ ions carried into Cu(NO₃)₂ are spectators: their nitrogen stays +5 throughout (+5 in HNO₃ → +5 in nitrate). No oxidation-state change means no electron transfer, so they are neither agent. This traps students who assume every nitrogen-containing species participates in the redox.

E) Cu²⁺ in Cu(NO₃)₂ is the oxidation PRODUCT. It contains copper, luring students who reason "copper is the reducer," but this copper has already lost its electrons (it is now +2) — an already-oxidized species is the conjugate oxidizing agent, not a reducing agent in this forward reaction.

stem:
A chemist electrolyses a 1 mol/L aqueous solution of sodium bromide (NaBr) using two inert platinum electrodes. To decide which species react, she uses the following standard reduction potentials:

  Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(s)                    E° = −2.71 V
  2 H₂O + 2 e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2 OH⁻        E° = −0.83 V
  Br₂ + 2 e⁻ → 2 Br⁻                  E° = +1.07 V
  O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H₂O           E° = +1.23 V

Given that reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode, and that the species most readily reduced (highest reduction potential) and most readily oxidized (lowest reduction potential) are favoured, which products form at each electrode?
choices: Cathode: H₂ gas; Anode: O₂ gas
Cathode: Na metal; Anode: O₂ gas
explanation:
At the cathode (reduction) the candidates are Na⁺ (E° = −2.71 V) and water (E° = −0.83 V). The higher (less negative) reduction potential is reduced preferentially, so water is reduced to H₂ gas, not Na⁺. At the anode (oxidation) the candidates are Br⁻ and water; the species with the LOWER reduction potential is oxidized more readily. Br₂/Br⁻ (+1.07 V) sits below O₂/H₂O (+1.23 V), so Br⁻ is oxidized to Br₂. Hence H₂ at the cathode and Br₂ at the anode — option A.

B (Na / Br₂): applies the 'molten NaCl' template to the cathode, reducing Na⁺ while ignoring that in water H₂O has the higher reduction potential and is reduced first.
C (H₂ / O₂): correctly reduces water but wrongly oxidizes water to O₂ — the trap of assuming O₂ always evolves, overlooking that Br⁻ has the lower reduction potential and is oxidized preferentially.
D (Br₂ / H₂): swaps the electrodes, confusing which electrode is oxidation vs reduction (electron-flow direction error): oxidation (Br₂) is placed at the cathode and reduction (H₂) at the anode.
E (Na / O₂): applies the fully aqueous-ignoring 'molten salt' picture to both electrodes, committing both the cathode error of B and the anode error of C simultaneously.

stem: The number of π (pi) bonds in an acyclic (ring-free) molecule can be obtained from its molecular formula: since no ring is present, every "degree of unsaturation" must correspond to exactly one π bond. For a neutral molecule the degree of unsaturation is D = (2·nC + 2 + nN − nH)/2, where nC, nN and nH are the numbers of carbon, nitrogen and hydrogen atoms (oxygen and the halogens do not enter the formula). Each of the five molecules below is acyclic and has a Lewis structure in which every atom obeys the octet rule (hydrogen the duet). Counting a double bond as one π bond and a triple bond as two π bonds, in which molecule do the atoms form a total of exactly TWO π bonds?
explanation:
Because each molecule is acyclic, its π-bond count equals its degree of unsaturation D = (2·nC + 2 + nN − nH)/2 (oxygen is ignored).

Correct — A) C₃H₄: D = (6 + 2 − 4)/2 = 2, so exactly two π bonds. This holds for either acyclic isomer: propyne HC≡C–CH₃ (a triple bond = two π bonds) or allene H₂C=C=CH₂ (two double bonds). The key insight is that a triple bond supplies two π bonds, so a single triple bond already gives the required total of two.

Distractor traps:
B) C₃H₆: D = (6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 1 — only one π bond (one C=C, e.g. propene). Chosen by students who undercount or confuse propene with propyne.
C) C₄H₁₀O: D = (8 + 2 − 10)/2 = 0 — a fully saturated alcohol/ether with all single bonds. Trap for students who assume that an oxygen atom must sit inside a C=O double bond; here the oxygen forms only single bonds.
D) C₄H₄: D = (8 + 2 − 4)/2 = 3 — three π bonds (e.g. vinylacetylene, one C=C plus one C≡C). Trap for students who count a triple bond as only one π bond: they get 1 + 1 = 2 and wrongly pick this.
E) C₄H₈O: D = (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1 — one π bond (a single C=O carbonyl, e.g. butanal/butanone). Trap for students who mistakenly count a double bond as two π bonds and so read 2.

Only A yields exactly two π bonds, and reaching it requires the correct rule that a triple bond = two π bonds while a double bond = one π bond.

stem: A pure organic compound is analysed and found to contain three elements in the following amounts per molecule: 8 carbon atoms, 10 hydrogen atoms, and 4 nitrogen atoms combined with 2 oxygen atoms. A chemist writes the molecular formula and then wishes to report the empirical formula (the formula with the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms). Which of the following is the correct empirical formula?
explanation:
The molecular formula is C₈H₁₀N₄O₂ (8 C, 10 H, 4 N, 2 O — this is caffeine, given here only as realistic context). To find the empirical formula, divide every subscript by the greatest common divisor of {8, 10, 4, 2}. The GCD is 2, giving C₄H₅N₂O — option A.

A) Correct: 8/2=4, 10/2=5, 4/2=2, 2/2=1 → C₄H₅N₂O.
B) Trap: reporting the molecular formula unchanged, failing to divide at all (the student who does not recognise that a common divisor exists).
C) Trap: dividing by 4 instead of the true GCD of 2. Using 4 works for C (8/4=2) and would-be O, but 10/4 and 4/4 are not both whole — the student forces C₂H₃NO by rounding 10/4→3 and ignoring that 4 does not divide 10. This encodes 'divide by the largest subscript's factor' without checking all subscripts.
D) Trap: dividing only C and H by 2 while leaving N and O untouched — applying the reduction inconsistently to only some elements.
E) Trap: dividing by the smallest subscript (2 for O) but mis-reducing, collapsing carbon to 1 (treating the smallest count as the divisor AND floor) — a student who over-reduces to force a '1' somewhere. The true GCD-based reduction never produces CH₂N₂O.

The item is selective because the divisor is 2 (not the give-away 'divide by 6' where the answer is obvious), four subscripts must all be tested against a common divisor, and each distractor corresponds to a distinct, plausible reduction error rather than a random number swap.

stem: A colourless liquid used as a rocket propellant is made of molecules with the formula X₂H₄. In each molecule the two X atoms are joined to each other by a single covalent bond, and every hydrogen atom forms exactly one covalent bond. Based only on this bonding information, what is the valency (number of covalent bonds) of each X atom?
explanation: Distribute the atoms by bonds. The 4 hydrogens each form one bond and are shared equally between the two X atoms, so each X forms 2 bonds to hydrogen. In addition, the two X atoms are joined to each other by one single covalent bond, adding 1 more bond to each X. Total per X = 2 + 1 = 3, so the valency of X is 3 (this molecule is hydrazine, N₂H₄). Distractor traps: (A) 1 counts only the shared X–X bond and forgets that each X also bonds to hydrogens. (B) 2 counts only the two bonds to hydrogen per X and ignores the X–X skeletal bond — the most tempting error. (D) 4 comes from misreading the formula as XH₄, putting all four hydrogens on a single X, or from assuming X must be tetravalent like carbon. (E) 5 is the total number of covalent bonds in the whole molecule (1 X–X + 4 X–H), mistaking a molecular bond count for a per-atom valency. Only 3 correctly balances the shared hydrogens with the X–X bond.

stem:
During the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), the planar tert-butyl carbocation formed in the first step reacts with a water molecule in the second step:

(CH₃)₃C⁺ + H₂O → (CH₃)₃C–OH₂⁺

Which statement correctly identifies the Lewis acid and the Lewis base in this step, together with a valid reason?
choices: The carbocation acts as the Lewis base because it actively seeks additional electrons.
Water acts as the Lewis acid because oxygen is more electronegative and withdraws electron density from the carbon.
Water acts as the Lewis base by donating a lone pair from oxygen into the empty orbital of the carbocation, which acts as the Lewis acid.
The carbocation acts as the Lewis base by donating its empty orbital to the oxygen atom of water.
No Lewis acid–base reaction occurs, because no proton (H⁺) is transferred between the two species.
explanation:
A Lewis base is an electron-pair DONOR; a Lewis acid is an electron-pair ACCEPTOR. The tert-butyl carbocation has an empty p orbital on the electron-deficient carbon, so it accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid). Water supplies one of its oxygen lone pairs to form the new C–O bond, so it is the electron-pair donor (Lewis base). Hence C is correct.

Trap in A: "seeks additional electrons" describes an ACCEPTOR — that is the definition of a Lewis acid, so the carbocation is mislabeled as a base (donor/acceptor role reversal).
Trap in B: it equates high electronegativity / electron-withdrawal with being a Lewis acid. Withdrawing electron density is not the same as accepting a donated lone pair to form a bond; water still contributes the electron pair, so it is the base, not the acid.
Trap in D: it reverses the mechanics of coordination — a species accepts a pair THROUGH an empty orbital, it does not "donate" an empty orbital. The carbocation is the acceptor (acid), not a donor.
Trap in E: it wrongly assumes Lewis acid–base chemistry requires proton transfer. That is the Brønsted definition; the Lewis definition covers lone-pair donation to form a coordinate (dative) bond, which is exactly what happens here even though no H⁺ moves.

stem: A chemist analyzes an unknown acyclic (non-cyclic, open-chain) hydrocarbon and determines that its molecular formula is C₅H₈. To identify the type of bonding present, she recalls that an acyclic alkane follows the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Based only on this information, which of the following statements about the unknown compound MUST be true?
choices: The molecule is fully saturated and contains only single bonds.
The molecule has a "degree of unsaturation" of 2, which — because it is acyclic — must come from either one triple bond or two double bonds.
The molecule must contain exactly one C=C double bond and no other multiple bonds.
The molecule has a degree of unsaturation of 1 and therefore contains a single C=C double bond.
The molecule must contain a ring, because only rings can reduce the hydrogen count below the saturated value.
explanation: For an acyclic alkane with n=5 carbons, the saturated formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ = C₅H₁₂. The unknown is C₅H₈, so it is missing 12−8 = 4 hydrogens. Each degree of unsaturation (one ring OR one double bond OR — counting twice — one triple bond) removes 2 H atoms, so 4 missing H corresponds to a degree of unsaturation of 2. Since the compound is stated to be acyclic, rings are excluded, so those 2 degrees must be supplied by carbon–carbon multiple bonds: either one triple bond (worth 2) or two double bonds (worth 1 each). That is exactly option B. Distractor A is the trap of comparing C₅H₈ to CₙH₂ₙ (thinking any deviation is 'still an alkane') — it wrongly calls the molecule saturated. Distractor C fixes on 'one double bond' but ignores that 2 degrees cannot be produced by a single double bond and forgets the triple-bond possibility. Distractor D is the most common error: dividing the H deficit wrong (using 2ₙ instead of 2ₙ+2, giving a deficit of 2 H and a degree of unsaturation of 1) — it undercounts by one full degree. Distractor E over-applies the ring rule and directly contradicts the given 'acyclic' condition, showing failure to read the constraint. Only B correctly computes the degree of unsaturation as 2 and correctly enumerates the acyclic possibilities.

stem:
The four organic compounds below all have very similar molar masses (58–62 g/mol):

• ethane-1,2-diol, HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH
• propan-1-ol, CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH
• propanal, CH₃–CH₂–CHO
• butane, CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃

Because their molar masses are almost equal, their London dispersion forces are comparable, so any difference in boiling point must come from the strongest additional intermolecular force present. Which sequence lists the four compounds in order of DECREASING boiling point (highest boiling point first)?
explanation:
Since molar masses (and therefore dispersion forces) are nearly equal, boiling point is set by the strongest extra intermolecular force. Ethane-1,2-diol has TWO O–H groups, giving the most extensive hydrogen-bonding network and the highest boiling point (~197 °C). Propan-1-ol has ONE O–H group, so it still hydrogen-bonds but less than the diol (~97 °C). Propanal has a polar C=O but no O–H, so it can only manage permanent dipole–dipole attraction, no hydrogen bonding (~49 °C). Butane is nonpolar, leaving dispersion forces alone as the weakest, so it boils lowest (~−1 °C). Correct order: diol > propan-1-ol > propanal > butane (A).

Distractor traps:
B — assumes the carbonyl (C=O) dipole is stronger than O–H hydrogen bonding, wrongly lifting propanal above propan-1-ol.
C — ranks the two hydrogen-bonding alcohols by carbon-chain length (i.e., by dispersion) instead of by the NUMBER of O–H groups, wrongly placing propan-1-ol above the diol.
D — inverts the force/boiling-point relationship, confusing ease of evaporation (volatility) with boiling point and giving the exact reverse order.
E — overvalues butane's dispersion (four carbons) and forgets that propanal has a permanent dipole, incorrectly swapping the bottom two. This is why simply "picking the nonpolar molecule as lowest" is not enough: propanal vs butane must be resolved with dipole–dipole reasoning.

stem: Two elements combine to form a single binary ionic compound. Element T has the ground-state electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹. Element Q lies in the same period as T, and a neutral Q atom needs to gain only one electron to become isoelectronic with a noble gas. Assuming each element adopts the ion charge predicted by its position in the periodic table, what is the empirical formula of the compound they form? (Formulas are written with the generic symbols T and Q.)
explanation:
Identify each ion from position, then balance charge. T has 13 electrons ([Ne]3s²3p¹) = aluminium, group 13; it loses all three valence electrons (3s² and 3p¹) to reach the [Ne] configuration, giving T³⁺. Q is in period 3 and needs to gain exactly one electron to be isoelectronic with a noble gas (18 e⁻ = Ar) — only chlorine fits, so Q is group 17 and forms Q⁻. Neutralizing charge: one T³⁺ needs three Q⁻, giving TQ₃ (correct, B).
Distractor traps: (A) TQ assumes T is only +1 — the misconception that the single 3p¹ electron gives a valence/charge of 1, pairing it with Q⁻. (C) T₃Q is the classic crossover error: the charge magnitudes are swapped onto the wrong atoms, writing T's 3 as T's subscript instead of Q's. (D) T₂Q₃ keeps T³⁺ correct but treats Q as Q²⁻ (mistaking "gains one electron" for a group-16 element that gains two), producing the M₂X₃ pattern. (E) TQ₂ takes Q⁻ correctly but counts only the 3s² electrons as T's valence, wrongly assigning T²⁺ and forgetting the 3p¹ electron.

stem: A technician prepares a stock solution by dissolving 8.0 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, molar mass = 40 g/mol) in water and adding water until the total volume is exactly 500 mL. She then withdraws a 50 mL portion of this stock solution and dilutes it with water to a final volume of 250 mL. What is the molarity of the final (diluted) solution?
explanation:
Three linked steps. (1) Convert mass to moles: n = 8.0 g / 40 g·mol⁻¹ = 0.20 mol. (2) Stock molarity: 0.20 mol / 0.500 L = 0.40 M. (3) Dilution (moles conserved, C₁V₁ = C₂V₂): C₂ = 0.40 M × (50 mL / 250 mL) = 0.40 × 0.20 = 0.080 M. Correct = A.
Distractor traps: B (0.40 M) stops at the stock concentration and forgets the dilution step entirely. C (0.80 M) treats all 0.20 mol as if dissolved in the final 250 mL, ignoring that only a 50 mL aliquot was taken (0.20/0.250). D (2.0 M) inverts the dilution ratio, multiplying by V_final/V_aliquot = 250/50 = 5 instead of dividing (0.40 × 5). E (3.2 M) skips the mass-to-moles conversion, treating 8.0 g as 8.0 mol: 8.0/0.5 = 16 M stock, then correctly diluted ×0.20 = 3.2 M. Each distractor encodes one specific, distinct error and none is also correct.

stem: A chemist stirs the compound Cl–CH=CH–CH2–Cl (1,3-dichloroprop-1-ene) with sodium cyanide (NaCN) in acetone. Numbering the chain so that C1 is the doubly-bonded carbon on the left bearing chlorine and C3 is the –CH2Cl group on the right, at which position does cyanide bring about nucleophilic substitution, and why?
choices: At the C1–Cl bond, because conjugation with the adjacent C=C activates that carbon toward nucleophilic attack.
At the C3–Cl bond, because C3 is an sp3 (saturated) carbon bearing a good leaving group.
At both C–Cl bonds at comparable rates, since each carbon carries an identical chloride leaving group.
At neither bond; cyanide instead adds across the C=C double bond, the molecule's most reactive site.
At the C1–Cl bond, because the greater s-character of the sp2 carbon makes it more electrophilic and therefore more reactive.
explanation: Nucleophilic substitution requires a saturated (sp3) electrophilic carbon carrying a good leaving group, where backside attack (SN2) or ionization (SN1) is geometrically feasible. In Cl–CH=CH–CH2Cl, C3 is the sp3 allylic –CH2Cl carbon; CN⁻ readily displaces Cl⁻ there, so B is correct. C1 is a vinylic sp2 carbon: its C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character (shorter and stronger), the electron-rich π system electrostatically repels the incoming anion, and the planar geometry blocks backside approach — so vinyl halides resist substitution. Trap A assumes conjugation activates a vinyl halide toward a nucleophile; it does not (that would require special vinylic-substitution conditions). Trap C assumes a leaving group alone is sufficient, ignoring that hybridization and geometry decide reactivity. Trap D confuses the nucleophile CN⁻ with an electrophile: an unactivated alkene undergoes electrophilic (not nucleophilic) addition, so CN⁻ does not add across C=C. Trap E wrongly equates higher s-character/electrophilicity with faster substitution, when in fact sp2 vinylic carbons are essentially inert to SN despite that.

stem: Under standard conditions (25 °C, 1 atm), the elements that occur as diatomic molecules (X₂) are usually thought of as gases. A chemistry student is challenged to name the ONE element that both (i) occurs naturally as discrete diatomic molecules and (ii) is a liquid under these same standard conditions. Which element satisfies BOTH requirements simultaneously?
explanation:
The item requires combining two facts: (1) which elements are diatomic and (2) their physical state at 25 °C/1 atm. Bromine (B) is the only element that is BOTH diatomic (Br₂) AND a liquid under standard conditions (mp −7 °C, bp 59 °C) — correct.

Distractor traps, each a distinct error path:
- A) Chlorine: correctly diatomic (Cl₂) but a GAS at standard conditions — the student remembers the diatomic property but ignores the state requirement.
- C) Iodine: correctly diatomic (I₂) but a SOLID at standard conditions — again the diatomic fact is right but the state is wrong (targets the assumption that halogens are liquids/gases).
- D) Mercury: correctly a LIQUID at standard conditions, but it is a monatomic metal, not diatomic — this is the sharpest trap, exploiting the well-known "two liquid elements at room temperature are Hg and Br" without checking the diatomic bonding condition.
- E) Sulfur: a nonmetal, so a student who over-generalizes "nonmetals are diatomic" may pick it; in fact sulfur is a polyatomic solid (S₈), satisfying neither condition.

Only bromine meets both criteria, so every distractor fails exactly one of the two requirements (or, for sulfur, both).

stem: A student places 0.10 mol of each of five different metals into five separate flasks, each containing a large excess of dilute sulfuric acid. Every reaction that can occur is allowed to run to completion, and the hydrogen gas produced in each flask is collected and measured at the same temperature and pressure. Which flask yields the greatest volume of hydrogen gas?
explanation: The general reaction is: active metal + dilute acid → salt + H₂. Two ideas must be combined: (1) only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react at all, and (2) the moles of H₂ released per mole of metal equal half the metal's ionic charge (each H₂ needs 2 electrons). With excess acid, the metal is limiting. Zn, Fe (→Fe²⁺ with dilute acid) and Mg are all divalent: 0.10 mol metal → 0.10 mol H₂. Aluminium is trivalent — 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂ — so 0.10 mol Al → 0.15 mol H₂, the greatest amount. Correct: E (aluminium), uniquely highest because 3 electrons per atom liberate more H₂ than any divalent metal here. Trap A (copper): the misconception that every metal reacts with acid; copper lies below hydrogen and gives no H₂ (0 mol). Trap B (zinc): defaulting to zinc because it is the textbook lab metal for preparing hydrogen — but it is divalent, only 0.10 mol. Trap C (iron): assuming iron behaves as Fe³⁺ and matches aluminium at 0.15 mol; with dilute acid iron oxidises only to Fe²⁺, giving 0.10 mol. Trap D (magnesium): confusing reactivity/reaction rate with quantity — magnesium is the most reactive here and fizzes fastest, but being divalent it still yields only 0.10 mol H₂; total volume depends on stoichiometry, not vigour.

stem: An organic compound Z has the condensed structure (CH₃)₃C–CH(OH)–CH₃. A chemist treats a sample of Z with warm acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which single statement correctly describes the classification of Z and the outcome of this reaction?
choices: Z is a tertiary alcohol, so it is not oxidised and no carbonyl compound forms.
Z is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a ketone.
Z is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a carboxylic acid.
Z is a primary alcohol, so it is oxidised to an aldehyde.
Z is a tertiary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a ketone.
explanation: The key step is identifying the hydroxyl-bearing (carbinol) carbon and counting the carbon atoms directly attached to IT — not to neighbouring atoms. In (CH₃)₃C–CH(OH)–CH₃ the carbinol carbon is the CH(OH) unit, which is bonded to exactly two other carbons: the terminal CH₃ and the quaternary C(CH₃)₃ carbon. Two carbon substituents means Z is a SECONDARY alcohol. Secondary alcohols are oxidised by acidified dichromate to ketones (here 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one), so B is correct. A: miscounts by attributing the three methyls of the bulky tert-butyl group to the carbinol carbon, wrongly calling Z tertiary; a tertiary alcohol would indeed resist oxidation, but Z is not tertiary. E: makes the same tertiary-misclassification AND compounds it with the misconception that tertiary alcohols oxidise to ketones (they do not oxidise at all). C: classifies Z correctly as secondary but assigns the primary-alcohol product — carboxylic acids come from oxidising primary alcohols, not secondary ones. D: undercounts the carbinol carbon's substituents as one, mistaking Z for a primary alcohol that would give an aldehyde. Only B gets both the classification (count = 2 → secondary) and the oxidation product (→ ketone) right.

stem:
A student is sorting five three-carbon compounds into functional-group classes. The condensed structural formulas are:

A. CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
B. CH₃CH₂CONH₂
C. CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂
D. CH₃CH₂COOH
E. CH₃CH₂CHO

Exactly one of these compounds belongs to the class of amines. Which one is it?
explanation: An amine is defined by an amino group (–NH₂, or >NH / >N–) in which the nitrogen is bonded only to carbon and hydrogen atoms — never to a carbonyl carbon. Only C, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (propan-1-amine), has nitrogen bonded to a saturated carbon and to hydrogens, so it is the amine. Distractor traps: A (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, propan-1-ol) carries the hydroxyl group –OH and is an alcohol — it catches students who blur the oxygen-based –OH with the nitrogen-based –NH₂. B (CH₃CH₂CONH₂, propanamide) is the key trap: it literally contains an –NH₂, so anyone who scans for the "NH₂" string picks it, but its nitrogen is attached to a carbonyl carbon (C=O), making it an amide, not an amine. D (CH₃CH₂COOH, propanoic acid) has the carboxyl group –COOH and is a carboxylic acid — it snares students who lump all polar/reactive groups together with amines. E (CH₃CH₂CHO, propanal) has the carbonyl group –CHO and is an aldehyde. Because every option is the same 3-carbon skeleton differing only in its functional group — and two options (B and C) both contain nitrogen — the item cannot be solved by counting atoms or spotting "N"; it requires correctly recognizing that the defining amine functionality is –NH₂ on a non-carbonyl carbon and distinguishing it from hydroxyl, carboxyl, carbonyl, and the amide.

stem: For a hydrocarbon, the degree of unsaturation, equal to (2C + 2 − H)/2, gives the number of rings plus the number of π bonds. Each species below is a stable, acyclic (ring-free) hydrocarbon, so ALL of its unsaturation must reside in carbon–carbon π bonds. Keeping in mind that double bonds may be placed on consecutive carbons (as in cumulenes such as H₂C=C=CH₂), for which molecular formula is it impossible to draw ANY acyclic structure that avoids a carbon–carbon triple bond?
explanation:
The key is that in an acyclic chain of n carbons there are only n − 1 carbon–carbon bonds, so at most n − 1 of them can be double bonds (a fully cumulated cumulene). A triple bond becomes unavoidable only when the required number of π bonds (the degree of unsaturation, since no rings are allowed) exceeds n − 1.

C) C₄H₂ — CORRECT. DoU = (8 + 2 − 2)/2 = 4. A 4-carbon chain has only 3 C–C bonds, so a maximum of 3 double bonds is possible (n − 1 = 3), which is fewer than the 4 π bonds required. At least one bond must be a triple bond (buta-1,3-diyne, HC≡C–C≡CH).

A) C₃H₆ — DoU = 1. A single C=C accounts for all unsaturation; a triple bond needs DoU ≥ 2, so one cannot even be present. Trap for choosing by surface appearance without computing DoU.

B) C₄H₆ — DoU = 2. Buta-1,3-diene (two separate double bonds) avoids any triple bond. Trap: equating "two degrees of unsaturation" with "a triple bond."

D) C₆H₆ — DoU = 4, the same value as the correct answer, but here n = 6 gives 5 available C–C bonds, so four double bonds fit easily (e.g., an acyclic hexatetraene); no triple bond is forced. Trap: matching DoU magnitude to the answer, or associating C₆H₆ with benzene's multiple bonds — this option isolates that what matters is DoU relative to n, and that "acyclic" excludes the aromatic ring.

E) C₄H₄ — DoU = 3. Butatriene, H₂C=C=C=CH₂, packs three cumulated double bonds into the 3 available C–C bonds with no triple bond. Trap: believing any DoU greater than 2 forces a triple bond, overlooking cumulenes; the strongest distractor.

stem:
Three compounds share the molecular formula C4H10O and therefore have the same molar mass (74 g/mol):

• Compound P: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (butan-1-ol)
• Compound Q: (CH3)3C-OH (2-methylpropan-2-ol)
• Compound R: CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3 (diethyl ether)

Because the three molecules are isomers, differences in their normal boiling points cannot be explained by molar mass. Using only the type of intermolecular forces each structure can form and the effect of molecular shape, which sequence correctly orders the compounds from HIGHEST to LOWEST boiling point?
explanation:
Since all three are isomers (identical molar mass), dispersion strength from mass is equalized, so only hydrogen-bond DONOR capability and molecular shape decide the order.

Step 1 — Hydrogen-bond donor: A molecule can hydrogen-bond to itself only if it has an H directly bonded to O (an O-H donor). Both alcohols P and Q have an O-H group, so both engage in strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Diethyl ether R has an oxygen but NO O-H bond — it is only a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so between R molecules the strongest force is ordinary dipole-dipole. Therefore both alcohols boil well above the ether: R is lowest.

Step 2 — Branching among the two alcohols: P and Q have equal mass and equal H-bonding capacity, so the tie-breaker is molecular shape. Butan-1-ol (P) is a straight chain with a large contact surface, maximizing London dispersion; 2-methylpropan-2-ol (Q) is compact and nearly spherical, minimizing surface contact. Less surface contact → weaker dispersion → lower boiling point. Thus P > Q.

Combined order: P > Q > R (option A). (Actual values: 118 °C, 82 °C, 35 °C.)

Trap in each distractor:
B (P > R > Q): correctly puts P first but over-weights branching — assumes the compact shape of Q hurts so much that Q falls below R, ignoring that Q still has an O-H donor (H-bonding) while R does not.
C (Q > P > R): correct that R is last, but reverses the branching effect — assumes the more branched/more substituted alcohol boils higher (confusing compactness or "more methyl groups" with stronger forces).
D (R > P > Q): the classic error of treating any oxygen as a hydrogen-bond donor — ranks the ether highest as if its lone-pair oxygen gave the strongest hydrogen bonding.
E (R > Q > P): combines both errors — ether treated as strongest H-bonder AND branching assumed to raise the boiling point — giving the fully inverted order.

stem: In a substitution reaction, the incoming group must act as a nucleophile — a species that donates an available lone pair of electrons to an electron-poor center. Considering both overall charge and the availability of a lone pair, which of the following species can act as a nucleophile?
explanation: A nucleophile must possess an AVAILABLE lone pair (or other readily donated electron density) to give to an electron-poor center; overall negative charge is neither necessary nor sufficient. C) N(CH₃)₃ (trimethylamine) is neutral yet the nitrogen carries a genuine, unshared lone pair, making it electron-rich — it donates that pair and is the nucleophile. Trap A) NH₄⁺: students associate nitrogen with nucleophilic amines, but here nitrogen's lone pair is already consumed in the fourth N–H bond and the ion is positively charged/electron-poor — no pair to donate. Trap B) CH₄: neutral like the answer, luring those who reason "neutral organic molecule = nucleophile," but it has only C–H σ bonds and no lone pair, so it cannot donate an electron pair. Trap D) BF₃: boron has an empty 2p orbital and is electron-deficient, so it ACCEPTS an electron pair — it is a Lewis acid/electrophile, the exact opposite of a nucleophile. Trap E) Mg²⁺: a cation with no lone pairs and a positive charge; it is electron-poor and behaves as a Lewis acid/electrophile, not a donor. Only C is electron-rich with an available lone pair. Note that the correct answer is neutral and no option is a nucleophilic anion, so the "pick the negative ion" shortcut fails.

stem: Four beakers each contain 0.20 mol of a single pure acid dissolved in water: acetic acid (CH₃COOH), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), and hydrochloric acid (HCl). Each solution is titrated to complete neutralization with a 0.50 mol·L⁻¹ NaOH solution. Which acid consumes the greatest volume of NaOH solution, and what is that volume?
explanation:
Complete neutralization consumes 1 mol NaOH per ionizable (acidic) proton, so moles of NaOH = 0.20 mol × proticity. The key step is reading proticity correctly from each formula: acetic acid is monoprotic (only the –COOH proton dissociates; the three C–H methyl hydrogens are NOT acidic), sulfuric acid is diprotic, phosphoric acid is triprotic, and hydrochloric acid is monoprotic. Thus NaOH required: CH₃COOH 0.20 mol, H₂SO₄ 0.40 mol, H₃PO₄ 0.60 mol, HCl 0.20 mol. The maximum is H₃PO₄ at 0.60 mol; volume = 0.60 mol ÷ 0.50 mol·L⁻¹ = 1.20 L = 1200 mL → C.

Distractor traps:
A) Counts all four hydrogens in CH₃COOH as ionizable (0.80 mol → 1600 mL), the classic error of confusing total formula H with acidic H.
B) Equates acid strength/the familiar diprotic H₂SO₄ with needing the most base; it actually consumes only 0.40 mol (800 mL), less than phosphoric acid.
D) Assumes the 'strongest' acid, HCl, must demand the most titrant; HCl is monoprotic, so only 0.20 mol → 400 mL.
E) Identifies the correct acid and the correct 0.60 mol of NaOH but ignores that the base is 0.50 M (divides by 1 M instead), giving 600 mL rather than 1200 mL.

stem:
A chemist runs four separate changes, each inside a well-insulated vessel immersed in a water bath, and records how the bath temperature responds:

• Process 1 — water vapour condensing onto a chilled coil: bath temperature RISES
• Process 2 — solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) subliming to gas: bath temperature FALLS
• Process 3 — molten candle wax solidifying: bath temperature FALLS
• Process 4 — propane burning in excess oxygen: bath temperature RISES

Heat exchange occurs only between the vessel contents (the system) and the surrounding water bath. Exactly ONE recorded bath-temperature change is inconsistent with the true sign of the system's enthalpy change, ΔH_sys, for that process. Identify that process and give the correct sign of its ΔH_sys.
explanation: Rule: an exothermic system (ΔH_sys < 0) releases heat, so the surrounding bath WARMS; an endothermic system (ΔH_sys > 0) absorbs heat, so the bath COOLS. Check each row. Process 1 (condensation) is exothermic — gas→liquid releases heat — so the bath rising is correct/consistent. Process 2 (sublimation) is endothermic — solid→gas absorbs heat — so the bath falling is correct/consistent. Process 3 (freezing/solidifying) is exothermic — liquid→solid releases heat — so the bath should RISE, but it was recorded as FALLING: this is the single inconsistent entry, and the correct sign is ΔH_sys < 0 (exothermic). Process 4 (combustion) is exothermic, so the bath rising is correct/consistent. Only Process 3 mismatches, making C correct. Trap A: flags condensation, encoding the classic error of confusing it with evaporation (thinking it is endothermic). Trap B: flags sublimation as exothermic, reversing the energy cost of separating molecules into the gas phase. Trap D: identifies the right process but assigns the wrong sign — the error of believing freezing absorbs heat (perhaps by analogy to melting). Trap E: flags combustion as endothermic, the misconception that because a spark/ignition energy is required the overall reaction must absorb energy. Only C names both the correct process and the correct sign.

stem: A chemist prepares an aqueous dispersion in which the dispersed particles have an average diameter of about 50 nm. To the naked eye the liquid looks completely clear (not cloudy). She then performs four tests: (1) shining a laser beam through the sample, (2) letting it stand undisturbed for several hours, (3) passing it through ordinary filter paper, and (4) passing it through a dialysis (semipermeable) membrane. Which single set of results is expected for this sample?
choices: The laser beam is invisible inside the liquid, and the particles pass freely through the dialysis membrane.
The laser beam is clearly visible as it crosses the liquid; the particles neither settle on standing nor pass through the dialysis membrane, yet they pass freely through the filter paper.
The laser beam is clearly visible, and the particles settle into a sediment on standing for a few hours.
The particles are retained by the ordinary filter paper and cannot pass through it.
The laser beam is invisible inside the liquid, but the particles are retained by the dialysis membrane.
explanation: A 50 nm particle diameter falls squarely in the colloidal range (roughly 1-1000 nm), so despite the clear appearance the sample is a colloid, not a true solution. The correct profile: particles this size scatter light, so the beam path is visible (Tyndall effect); they are kept dispersed by Brownian motion and do NOT settle; they are far smaller than filter-paper pores (~micrometers) so they pass through filter paper; but they are too large to cross a dialysis membrane. That is exactly option B. Trap A treats "clear to the eye" as proof of a true solution (no Tyndall, membrane-permeable), but transparency does not exclude colloidal dimensions above 1 nm. Trap C correctly reads the positive Tyndall result but wrongly infers a suspension that settles; colloidal particles scatter light yet remain suspended. Trap D assumes colloidal particles are big enough to be caught by filter paper, confusing filter-paper pores with membrane pores; only suspensions (>1000 nm) are retained by filter paper. Trap E is internally inconsistent: it assumes the particles are small enough to give no scattering (solution-like) yet large enough to be blocked by a membrane (colloid-like), mixing the two size regimes.

topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
stem:
A species is especially stable when it attains the electron configuration of a noble gas — a completely filled outer shell identical to that of an atom in Group 18. Consider the following neutral atoms and monatomic ions:

Ca,  Fe³⁺,  K⁺,  Zn²⁺,  Br

Working out the electron count and resulting configuration of each, which ONE already possesses a complete outer shell identical to that of a noble gas?
explanation:
The competency is recognizing a genuine noble-gas (complete-outer-shell) configuration, here made selective by requiring the student to compute electron counts for ions and to distinguish a true noble-gas configuration from look-alikes.

Correct — C) K⁺: Potassium is Z = 19; removing one electron gives 18 electrons → [Ar] = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶. This is a complete octet identical to argon, a real noble gas. This is the only species that reaches a genuine noble-gas configuration.

Distractor traps:
• A) Ca (Z = 20): [Ar]4s² — the outer shell holds only 2 electrons, not a full octet. Trap: assuming a reactive metal is already stable; Ca becomes noble-gas-like only after losing 2 electrons (as Ca²⁺), not as the neutral atom.
• B) Fe³⁺ (26 − 3 = 23 e⁻): [Ar]3d⁵ — a half-filled d subshell has modest extra stability but is NOT a noble-gas configuration. Trap: confusing half-filled-subshell stability with a complete outer shell.
• D) Zn²⁺ (30 − 2 = 28 e⁻): [Ar]3d¹⁰ — a completely filled d subshell (a "pseudo-noble-gas" core), but it is not identical to any noble gas; the next noble gas, krypton, is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶. Trap: mistaking a filled d¹⁰ for a genuine noble-gas outer shell.
• E) Br (Z = 35): [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p⁵ — a halogen that is one electron short of a filled outer shell. Trap: picking the element "closest" to a noble gas; only the anion Br⁻ attains the octet, not neutral Br.

stem: A main-group element X in Period 4 forms a volatile hydride with the formula H2X, and in its highest oxidation state it forms an oxide with the formula XO3. Based only on this chemical behaviour, how many valence electrons does an atom of X have?
explanation: Both clues must be combined and both must point to the same group. The hydride H2X shows X gains/shares 2 electrons to complete an octet, giving a lowest oxidation state of -2. The highest oxide XO3 shows X reaches an oxidation state of +6 (as in SO3). An element whose maximum positive oxidation state is +6 sits in Group 16 (the chalcogens, e.g. selenium in Period 4), and a Group-16 atom has 6 valence electrons — answer C. Distractor A (2) mistakes the two hydrogen atoms in H2X for the valence-electron count, reading stoichiometry as valence. Distractor B (4) confuses the period number (4) with the number of valence electrons. Distractor D (8) assumes the atom already possesses a full octet rather than the 6 electrons it has before bonding. Distractor E (16) takes the modern 18-column group number (16) directly as the valence count instead of converting it (16 - 10 = 6). Only C reconciles the -2 hydride and +6 oxide with the correct group.

stem: During a laboratory session, students are told that a homogeneous mixture consists of a SINGLE phase with uniform composition throughout — no boundaries between different phases remain, even when the sample is examined under a microscope. Each student then classifies one everyday system. Which student's sample is genuinely a homogeneous mixture?
choices: Brass, a solid alloy in which zinc atoms are dissolved among copper atoms to form a single solid solution
Whole milk, which looks uniformly white to the naked eye but disperses tiny fat droplets throughout a watery liquid
Fog, a single visible cloud of grey air in which fine liquid water droplets remain suspended
A polished slab of granite, one solid block containing interlocked grains of quartz, feldspar, and mica
A glass of freshly poured sparkling water, a clear liquid through which streams of carbon-dioxide bubbles rise
explanation: The defining criterion is a SINGLE phase with uniform composition at the microscopic level, not merely a uniform appearance to the eye. (A) Brass is a substitutional solid solution: zinc atoms sit within a single copper lattice, giving one solid phase of uniform composition — a homogeneous mixture (correct). The trap is thinking a metal cannot be a mixture; alloys are the classic solid homogeneous mixtures. (B) Milk trap = 'uniform white color means homogeneous'; it is a colloidal emulsion with fat droplets forming a distinct dispersed phase, so it is heterogeneous. (C) Fog trap = 'one visible cloud of air is one phase'; suspended liquid droplets are a second phase (an aerosol), making it heterogeneous. (D) Granite trap = 'a single solid block is homogeneous'; distinct visible mineral grains are separate solid phases, so it is heterogeneous. (E) Sparkling water trap = 'a clear solution must be homogeneous'; the rising CO2 bubbles are a gas phase coexisting with the liquid, giving two phases — heterogeneous at that moment.

stem:
When sodium dihydrogen phosphate dissolves in water, the ion H₂PO₄⁻ is amphiprotic: in some reactions it donates a proton, and in others it accepts one. A student writes the equation for H₂PO₄⁻ acting purely as a Brønsted–Lowry ACID toward water:

  H₂PO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ (conjugate base) + (species X)

Considering ONLY this acid behaviour, which choice correctly gives the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
choices: HPO₄²⁻ — formed when H₂PO₄⁻ donates one proton
H₃PO₄ — formed when H₂PO₄⁻ accepts one proton
PO₄³⁻ — formed when H₂PO₄⁻ donates two protons
OH⁻ — since a base must be a source of hydroxide ions
H₃O⁺ — the species produced when H₂PO₄⁻ reacts as an acid with water
explanation: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid donates exactly ONE proton, keeping the same skeleton. Here H₂PO₄⁻ (charge −1) loses one H⁺ to become HPO₄²⁻ (charge −2): correct is A. Trap B (H₃PO₄) is the conjugate ACID — it comes from ACCEPTING a proton, exploiting the fact that an amphiprotic ion can go either way; a student who ignores the stated "acting as an acid" direction picks it. Trap C (PO₄³⁻) removes TWO protons, confusing "conjugate base" with "fully deprotonated form." Trap D (OH⁻) is the classic Arrhenius misconception that any base must supply hydroxide, ignoring the Brønsted proton-transfer definition. Trap E (H₃O⁺) correctly identifies species X in the equation but mislabels it: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of water, not the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻ — it is the wrong member of the two conjugate pairs. Only A follows the single-proton-removal rule in the specified acid direction.

stem:
Five main-group elements are represented by the fictitious symbols Q, R, T, X and Z. For each element the table below gives the formula of its HIGHEST oxide and of its SIMPLEST hydrogen compound (hydride):

  Element | Highest oxide | Simplest hydride
  --------+---------------+-----------------
     Q    |     Q₂O       |       QH
     R    |     RO₃       |       H₂R
     T    |     T₂O₇      |       HT
     X    |     X₂O₅      |       XH₃
     Z    |     ZO₂       |       ZH₄

A separate sample of each element is allowed to react with the same Group 1 alkali metal M. Which element forms a stable ionic compound with M in a 1 : 1 atomic ratio (general formula MW)?
explanation:
Reasoning path: for a main-group element the formula of the highest oxide fixes the maximum positive oxidation state, which equals the number of valence electrons and therefore the group. Q₂O → max +1 → Group 1 (alkali metal); RO₃ → max +6 → Group 16 (chalcogen); T₂O₇ → max +7 → Group 17 (halogen); X₂O₅ → max +5 → Group 15 (pnictogen); ZO₂ → max +4 → Group 14. The alkali metal M forms M⁺. A 1:1 ionic compound MW therefore requires W to carry a single −1 charge, i.e. to gain exactly one electron to reach an octet — the defining reactivity of a halogen (7 valence electrons). Only T fits: its highest oxide T₂O₇ and its hydride HT (the HX pattern) both mark it as Group 17, so M⁺T⁻ = MT (1:1). Answer C.

Distractor traps:
A) Q is itself a metal (Group 1, Q₂O, QH, forms Q⁺). Two metals do not form a simple ionic compound, and its 1:1 hydride QH baits students into transferring "1:1 with hydrogen" to "1:1 with M." It also exploits the alkali-metal/halogen "both extremely reactive" confusion.
B) R is the chalcogen (RO₃, H₂R): it gains TWO electrons (−2), giving M₂R (2:1), not 1:1. This is the central halogen-vs-chalcogen discrimination the item targets — the near-neighbour that only differs by one valence electron.
D) X is a pnictogen (X₂O₅, XH₃): −3 ion → M₃X (3:1). Trap for students who misread the odd-looking X₂O₅ as the halogen's X₂O₇.
E) Z is a Group-14 element (ZO₂, ZH₄): it bonds mainly covalently (or notionally −4), and does not form a 1:1 ionic compound with M⁺. Trap: the symmetric ZO₂/ZH₄ formulas suggest a simple 1:1 pairing.

stem:
The table lists three standard molar energies for water, each corresponding to a different physical or chemical change:

  • Melting ice, H2O(s) → H2O(l):        +6 kJ/mol
  • Boiling water, H2O(l) → H2O(g):       +41 kJ/mol
  • Atomising the vapour, H2O(g) → 2 H(g) + O(g):  +926 kJ/mol

All three values are positive because each change requires energy to pull particles apart. Which interpretation of these three numbers is correct?
choices: Melting and boiling only overcome intermolecular hydrogen bonds, leaving each molecule intact, whereas the 926 kJ/mol reflects breaking the two O–H covalent bonds; the large gap shows that intermolecular forces are far weaker than the covalent bonds within a molecule.
The rising sequence 6 → 41 → 926 kJ/mol shows three progressively stronger varieties of hydrogen bond, from the weak bonds in ice to the strongest bonds in isolated gas atoms.
Boiling needs more energy than melting because covalent O–H bonds are broken during boiling but not during melting, which is why steam is chemically different from liquid water.
The 926 kJ/mol value measures the strength of hydrogen bonding in the gas phase, which is greater than in the liquid because gas molecules move faster and collide harder.
Because 41 kJ/mol is already needed just to boil water, each individual hydrogen bond must be stronger than each O–H covalent bond, since many molecules must be separated at once.
explanation:
The key competency is distinguishing intermolecular forces (broken on melting/boiling) from intramolecular covalent bonds (broken only on atomisation), and ranking their strengths. Melting (6) and boiling (41) merely separate whole H2O molecules by overcoming hydrogen bonds; the molecules survive with their O–H bonds intact. Atomising the vapour (926 ≈ 2 × 463) actually severs the covalent O–H bonds. The ~20-fold gap between 41 and 926 is direct evidence that intermolecular forces are much weaker than covalent bonds — the correct reading (A).
B (trap: treats every energy as a 'hydrogen bond', so a student who never separates IMF from covalent bonding sees one continuous scale of H-bond strengths — but 926 is covalent, not any kind of H-bond). C (trap: the classic misconception that boiling breaks covalent bonds; if it did, steam would be H and O atoms, not H2O — boiling only overcomes IMFs, which is why steam is still water). D (trap: invents 'gas-phase hydrogen bonding' and misreads the atomisation value as an IMF; isolated gas molecules are already separated, so no intermolecular energy remains — 926 is intramolecular). E (trap: inverted ranking — reasoning that because boiling costs 41 kJ/mol the H-bonds must be strong; per-interaction the hydrogen bond (~20 kJ/mol) is roughly 20× weaker than an O–H bond (~463 kJ/mol), and 'many molecules at once' does not make each bond stronger).

stem:
Four elements are labelled G, J, M and Q. Their Pauling electronegativity (EN) values and their metallic or non-metallic character are given below:

  • G — EN = 0.8 — metal
  • J — EN = 1.2 — metal
  • M — EN = 2.5 — non-metal
  • Q — EN = 3.4 — non-metal

A bond's predominant type is predicted from BOTH the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) between the two bonded atoms AND whether the atoms are metals or non-metals. On this basis, which statement correctly predicts the predominant bond type between a pair of these elements?
choices: G bonded to J gives a polar covalent bond.
G bonded to Q gives an ionic compound.
M bonded to Q gives an ionic compound.
J bonded to M gives a metallic bond.
G bonded to J gives an ionic compound.
explanation: The rule needs two inputs: ΔEN and the metal/non-metal character of the partners. Correct (B): G is a metal (0.8) and Q a non-metal (3.4); ΔEN = 2.6 is large, so electrons are transferred → ionic. Trap A: G–J has a small ΔEN (0.4), so a student who uses ΔEN alone calls it covalent — but both atoms are metals, so the bond is metallic, not polar covalent. Trap E: same G–J pair; the misconception here is that two different metals with any EN difference must transfer electrons to form ions — again, two metals give a metallic (delocalised) bond, not ionic. Trap C: M and Q are both strongly electronegative, tempting "high EN → ionic," but they are two non-metals and ΔEN is only 0.9, so electrons are shared → (polar) covalent, not ionic. Trap D: J–M contains a metal (J), and the misconception is "if a metal is present the bond is metallic"; metallic bonding requires ALL partners to be metals — here a metal bonds a non-metal (ΔEN = 1.3), giving a polar covalent/ionic bond, never metallic. Only B satisfies both criteria (large ΔEN AND metal + non-metal).

topic: Chemistry — Periodic Table and Atomic Structure
stem: A researcher lists the ground-state electron configurations of five neutral elements but hides their names. To decide which sample could form a coloured ion with variable oxidation states, she first needs to identify the one element that is a true transition metal. Based only on the configurations below, which element is the transition metal?
explanation:
A transition metal is defined by a partially (incompletely) filled d subshell in the atom or in one of its common ions. Option B is [Ar]3d⁶4s² (iron): the 3d subshell is partially filled, so it is a genuine d-block transition metal that forms coloured ions with variable oxidation states — the correct answer.

Distractor traps:
A) [Ar]4s¹ (potassium): a reactive metal, but its valence electron is in the s subshell — it is an s-block main-group (alkali) metal, no d electrons at all. Trap: equating "reactive metal" with "transition metal."
C) [Ar]3d¹⁰4s² (zinc): it sits in the d-block columns, but the 3d subshell is completely full (d¹⁰) and Zn²⁺ is also d¹⁰, so by the partially-filled-d criterion it is NOT a transition metal. Trap: assuming any element containing 3d electrons is a transition metal.
D) [Ar]3d¹⁰4s²4p¹ (gallium): the 3d core is complete and the highest-energy (valence) electron enters the 4p subshell, making it a p-block main-group metal. Trap: seeing "3d¹⁰" and ignoring that the defining valence electron is in p.
E) [Ne]3s²3p⁴ (sulfur): a p-block nonmetal with no d electrons — disqualified on two counts (not a metal, not d-block). Trap: skimming the configuration without checking metal character.

stem: The complete Lewis structure of a polyatomic ion is shown below, with all lone pairs on the central atom drawn explicitly (peripheral-atom lone pairs are omitted for clarity). Based only on the electron domains you can count around the central iodine atom, what is the molecular shape of this ion and the approximate value of a single Cl–I–Cl bond angle between two adjacent bonded chlorine atoms?
choices: Square planar, with adjacent Cl–I–Cl angles of about 90°
Tetrahedral, with Cl–I–Cl angles of about 109.5°
Octahedral, with Cl–I–Cl angles of about 90°
Square pyramidal, with Cl–I–Cl angles slightly less than 90°
See-saw, with Cl–I–Cl angles of about 90° and 120°
explanation: Counting the domains drawn in the figure: the central I has 4 bonding domains (to the four Cl) plus 2 lone pairs = 6 total electron domains. Six domains adopt an octahedral electron-domain arrangement; the two lone pairs take opposite (trans, axial) positions to minimize repulsion, leaving the four Cl in one plane. This gives an AX₄E₂ molecular shape = square planar, with adjacent Cl–I–Cl angles of 90° (A, correct). B (tetrahedral, 109.5°) ignores both lone pairs and counts only the 4 bonds as AX₄ — the classic 'shape from atoms only' error. C (octahedral) counts all 6 domains correctly but names the electron-domain geometry as the molecular shape, forgetting that lone pairs are not part of the reported shape. D (square pyramidal) reads only ONE lone pair from the figure (AX₅E, an octahedral parent with 1 lone pair), misreading the drawn structure. E (see-saw) undercounts the total to 5 domains (AX₄E, trigonal-bipyramidal parent), losing one lone pair entirely. Only a correct count of 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs read from the figure yields the square-planar answer.

stem: A monatomic ion is found to contain 24 protons, 28 neutrons, and 21 electrons. A student is asked to state the ion's overall charge and to explain how the ion formed from its neutral parent atom. Which of the following statements is entirely correct?
choices: The ion has a charge of 3+ because it contains three more protons than electrons, so it formed when the neutral atom lost 3 electrons.
The ion has a charge of 3− because subtracting the 24 protons from the 21 electrons gives −3, so it formed when the neutral atom gained 3 electrons.
The ion has a charge of 7+ because it contains seven more neutrons than electrons (28 − 21 = 7).
The ion has a charge of 4+ because it contains four more neutrons than protons (28 − 24 = 4), and this excess of mass makes it positive.
The ion is electrically neutral overall because its 3 extra neutrons cancel out the imbalance between the protons and the electrons.
explanation: Net charge is set only by protons (positive) versus electrons (negative); neutrons are electrically neutral and never enter the count. Charge = (protons) − (electrons) = 24 − 21 = +3, so the ion is a 3+ cation. A neutral parent atom of this element has 24 electrons (to match its 24 protons); having only 21 electrons means 3 electrons were lost, which is exactly how a cation forms — making A correct. B encodes the sign-convention error: it computes electrons − protons and misreads the deficit of electrons as a gain, wrongly producing a 3− anion (in fact fewer electrons must give a positive ion). C uses neutrons − electrons (28 − 21 = 7), the misconception that neutrons carry or contribute to charge. D uses neutrons − protons (28 − 24 = 4) and the false idea that a neutron/mass excess creates positive charge; neutron count is irrelevant to charge. E reflects the misconception that neutrons neutralize a proton/electron imbalance, but neutral particles cannot offset a real charge difference, so the ion is not neutral.

stem:
A student records four processes in the laboratory and notes whether each releases heat to the surroundings or absorbs heat from them:

1. Solid ammonium nitrate is stirred into water; the beaker becomes noticeably cold to the touch.
2. Water vapour on a cold window collects into liquid droplets, and the glass warms slightly.
3. Powdered magnesium is ignited in air and burns with a bright flame, giving off intense heat.
4. Liquid butane sprayed from a can evaporates instantly, cooling the metal nozzle.

The student must sort these into a single category that is BOTH "a genuine chemical reaction" AND "exothermic" (releases heat because the net energy of bonds formed exceeds that of bonds broken). Which statement correctly identifies that category and justifies it?
choices: Only process 3 qualifies: new chemical bonds form in magnesium oxide, and the large energy released on forming those bonds makes it exothermic; processes 2 and 4 are physical phase changes and process 1 is an endothermic dissolution.
Processes 2 and 3 both qualify, because each releases heat and any process that warms its surroundings is by definition a chemical reaction.
Only process 2 qualifies: condensation forms new bonds between water molecules and releases heat, so it is an exothermic chemical reaction.
Only process 1 qualifies, because dissolving a solid always breaks chemical bonds and any heat change during dissolving counts as an exothermic reaction.
Processes 3 and 4 both qualify, because both involve a substance changing state while releasing the energy stored in its chemical bonds.
explanation:
The correct category requires two independent conditions to be met at once: the process must be a true chemical reaction (new substances/bonds formed, not just a phase change or mixing) AND it must be exothermic (heat released because bonds formed release more energy than bonds broken require).

Evaluating each process: (1) NH4NO3 dissolving is a PHYSICAL dissolution and it is ENDOTHERMIC (beaker gets cold), so it fails both tests. (2) Water vapour condensing releases heat, but it is a PHYSICAL phase change (gas to liquid) — no new chemical bonds form, only intermolecular attractions — so it is exothermic but NOT a reaction. (3) Mg + O2 to MgO forms genuinely new chemical bonds and releases large energy (bonds formed >> bonds broken), so it is both a chemical reaction AND exothermic — it alone qualifies. (4) Butane evaporating is a PHYSICAL phase change that is ENDOTHERMIC (absorbs heat, cools the nozzle), failing both tests.

A is correct: it selects only process 3 and correctly classifies the other three.

Distractor traps:
B encodes the misconception that "warms the surroundings" is sufficient to call something a reaction — it wrongly promotes physical condensation (2) to a reaction and conflates heat direction with chemical change.
C encodes the trap of calling condensation an exothermic "reaction" by mislabeling intermolecular attraction formation as chemical bond formation — a physical change misclassified as chemical.
D encodes the misconception that dissolving breaks chemical bonds and that any heat change during dissolving is exothermic — it both mislabels a physical process as chemical and ignores that process 1 is actually endothermic.
E encodes the misconception that phase changes release "stored chemical bond energy," wrongly grouping combustion (3, a real exothermic reaction) with butane evaporation (4, an endothermic physical change) and treating both as the same category.

stem: The molecule 1,2-butadiene has the condensed structure CH₂=C=CH–CH₃, a chain in which two consecutive carbon–carbon double bonds share a common central carbon. Number the carbons C1–C4 from left to right, so that C1 is the terminal =CH₂ group and C4 is the terminal –CH₃ group. Exactly one carbon in this molecule has a linear (180°) local geometry, forming two sigma bonds together with two pi bonds. Which carbon is sp-hybridized?
explanation: Hybridization is set by the number of sigma bonds (equal to the number of neighboring atoms) around a carbon; sp means exactly two sigma bonds plus two pi bonds, giving linear 180° geometry. C2 is bonded to only two atoms (C1 and C3), forming 2 sigma bonds, and it carries one pi bond toward each neighbor (2 pi bonds total) — so it is sp and linear. This is the key insight: an sp carbon need not sit in a triple bond; the central carbon of a cumulated diene qualifies. Distractor traps: A (C1) is the =CH₂ carbon, which forms 3 sigma bonds (two C–H, one C–C) + 1 pi → sp², ~120°; picking it reflects the misconception that any doubly-bonded terminal carbon is sp. C (C3) forms 3 sigma bonds (C–H, C–C2, C–C4) + 1 pi → sp², the trap of labeling an internal alkene carbon sp. D (C4) is CH₃ with 4 sigma bonds and no pi → sp³, chosen by students who think adjacency to the unsaturated chain changes its hybridization. E encodes the blanket error "carbons in double bonds are sp" — but both C1 and C3 have three sigma bonds and are sp², not sp.

stem: The velocity–time graph shows an electric tram during a 16 s test run along a straight track. The run consists of three distinct phases of motion. During the phase in which the tram's (uniform) acceleration is greatest, what is the magnitude of that acceleration? (Read all required values from the graph.)
explanation: Acceleration is the slope of the velocity–time line over a segment, a = Δv/Δt. The three phases have slopes: Phase 1 (0–4 s, 0→6 m/s) = 6/4 = 1.5 m/s²; Phase 2 (4–10 s, 6→24 m/s) = 18/6 = 3.0 m/s²; Phase 3 (10–16 s, constant 24 m/s) = 0. The steepest segment is Phase 2, so the greatest acceleration is 3.0 m/s² → D. Distractor traps: A (1.5 m/s²) reads the slope of Phase 1 — the wrong (less steep) segment, mistaking the first visible ramp for the steepest. B (1.8 m/s²) takes the correct Δv = 18 m/s of Phase 2 but divides by the total elapsed clock time 10 s instead of the segment duration Δt = 6 s. C (2.4 m/s²) divides the endpoint velocity 24 m/s by its clock time 10 s (a slope-from-the-origin error, ignoring that Phase 2 does not start at t=0, v=0). E (4.0 m/s²) uses the segment's final velocity 24 m/s over its duration 6 s, forgetting to subtract the initial velocity 6 m/s (uses final v instead of Δv). Only D correctly identifies the steepest segment AND reads both of its endpoints.

stem: A cyclist records her speed during a one‑hour training ride. The velocity–time graph below shows three consecutive phases, each ridden at a constant speed. The time axis is marked in minutes and the speed axis in km/h. Reading the values from the graph, what total distance does she cover during the full hour?
explanation:
Distance equals the area under a velocity–time graph, and each phase duration (in minutes) must be converted to hours. Phase 1: 30 km/h for 20 min = 30 × (20/60) = 10 km. Phase 2: 48 km/h for 30 min = 48 × (30/60) = 24 km. Phase 3: 12 km/h for 10 min = 12 × (10/60) = 2 km. Total = 10 + 24 + 2 = 36 km (option D).

Distractor traps:
- A) 24 km: reports only the largest single area (the 48 km/h phase), treating the dominant segment as the whole ride and discarding the other two phases.
- B) 30 km: takes the unweighted mean of the three speeds, (30 + 48 + 12)/3 = 30 km/h, times the full 1 h — ignoring that the phases have unequal durations.
- C) 34 km: computes the first two areas correctly (10 + 24) but drops the final low-speed 10-minute phase, forgetting its 2 km.
- E) 48 km: assumes the peak speed (48 km/h) is held for the entire hour (48 × 1 h) — reading only the maximum value instead of summing the phase areas.

The item is unsolvable from the text alone: all speeds and phase durations appear only in the figure, and the answer requires reading three areas and applying the min→hour conversion to each.

stem: In a workshop, two pulleys are joined by a taut, non-slipping belt that runs around their rims. The large drive pulley has a radius of 15 cm and completes one full turn every 0.40 s. The small driven pulley has a radius of 5.0 cm. Assuming the belt does not slip, what is the rotational frequency of the small driven pulley?
explanation: A non-slipping belt forces the rim (tangential) speed of both pulleys to be equal: v = 2*pi*r*f is the same for each, so f_small = f_large * (r_large / r_small). First convert the drive pulley's period to frequency using the reciprocal relation f = 1/T = 1/0.40 = 2.5 Hz. Then f_small = 2.5 * (15/5) = 2.5 * 3 = 7.5 Hz (A, correct). Because the smaller pulley must turn faster to keep pace with the belt, its frequency exceeds the drive pulley's. Distractor B (2.5 Hz) assumes both pulleys share the same frequency, ignoring the belt/radius constraint. Distractor C (1.2 Hz) applies the correct 3:1 radius ratio but forgets to invert the period, using 0.40 * 3 = 1.2 instead of first converting T to f. Distractor D (0.83 Hz) inverts the radius ratio (r_small/r_large), the common belief that the larger pulley spins faster: 2.5 * (5/15). Distractor E (0.13 Hz) computes the small pulley's period (T_small = 0.40/3 = 0.133 s) and mislabels that time as a frequency, confusing period with its reciprocal.

stem: A drone flies in a straight line described by displacement vector a, then immediately changes course and flies along displacement vector b. The two displacements are drawn tip-to-tail on the coordinate grid below, where each square represents 1 km. Using the grid to read each vector's components, what is the magnitude and direction of the drone's total (resultant) displacement from its starting point?
explanation: From the grid, a = (8, 0) km and b = (−3, +4) km (b points up and to the LEFT). Because the vectors are joined tip-to-tail, the resultant runs from the tail of a to the head of b: R = a + b = (8−3, 0+4) = (5, 4) km. Its magnitude is √(5² + 4²) = √41 ≈ 6.4 km, at an angle atan(4/5) ≈ 39° above the +x axis. This requires resolving into components and honoring b's direction — the crux of vectors carrying both magnitude and direction. Trap A (13 km along +x): adds the magnitudes as scalars (8 + 5), ignoring direction entirely. Trap B (11.7 km, 20°): reads b's leftward x-component with the wrong sign, using b = (+3, +4) → R = (11, 4), so it treats magnitude as if direction can be dropped from the x-component. Trap D (9.4 km, 32°): treats a and b as if perpendicular, computing √(|a|² + |b|²) = √(8² + 5²) = √89 ≈ 9.4 km — valid only for right-angle vectors, which these are not. Trap E (3 km along +x): subtracts the magnitudes (8 − 5), the misconception that the vectors partially cancel to a scalar difference along a's direction.

stem: The diagram is a top-down (bird's-eye) view of a 6 kg block resting on a frictionless horizontal surface. Gravity and the normal force act perpendicular to this view and are not shown, so only the three horizontal forces F₁, F₂, and F₃ drawn in the figure affect the block's motion. Using sin 37° = 0.6 and cos 37° = 0.8, what is the magnitude of the block's acceleration?
explanation:
The forces must be resolved into components using the geometry in the figure. F₁ = 60 N acts at 37° above the +x axis, so F₁ₓ = 60(0.8) = 48 N and F₁ᵧ = 60(0.6) = 36 N. F₂ = 24 N points in −x and F₃ = 18 N points in −y. Net components: Fₓ = 48 − 24 = 24 N, Fᵧ = 36 − 18 = 18 N. Net force = √(24² + 18²) = √900 = 30 N. Then a = F_net/m = 30/6 = 5 m/s² → C.

Distractor traps:
A) 3 m/s²: treats the three forces as collinear scalars and subtracts magnitudes, (60 − 24 − 18)/6 = 3 — ignores the 37° geometry entirely (also the value you get if you keep only the vertical net, 18/6).
B) 4 m/s²: resolves horizontally correctly but forgets the vertical forces contribute to the net, using only Fₓ = 24 N → 24/6 = 4 (incomplete 2D resolution).
D) 10 m/s²: uses only the applied force F₁ = 60 N and ignores the two opposing forces, 60/6 = 10 (forgets F₂ and F₃ exist).
E) 15 m/s²: decomposes F₁ but misreads F₂ and F₃ as aiding rather than opposing, adding instead of subtracting: √(72² + 54²)/6 = 90/6 = 15 (sign/direction error).

stem: A ball of mass 4 kg falls vertically and passes point B (a window) on the side of a tall building, as shown in the figure. The ball's speed as it passes B and the height of B above the ground are marked in the figure. Air resistance is negligible and g = 10 m/s². Using the values shown, what is the ball's kinetic energy at the instant just before it strikes the ground?
explanation: n/a

stem: In the SI system, kilogram (kg), metre (m), second (s) and ampere (A) are base units, while units such as the newton, joule, pascal, watt and coulomb are derived and can be written entirely in terms of the base units. Each option below claims to express one derived unit purely in base units. Using the defining relationships force = mass × acceleration, pressure = force ÷ area, work = force × distance, power = work ÷ time, and electric charge = current × time, identify the single decomposition that is correct.
explanation:
Build each unit from base units. Force: N = kg·m·s⁻². Pressure = force ÷ area = (kg·m·s⁻²) ÷ m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻², so option C is correct.

Each distractor encodes a specific misconception:
A) newton = kg·m²·s⁻² is wrong — that expression is actually the joule. It comes from treating force as if it already included a distance factor (confusing force with energy).
B) joule = kg·m·s⁻² is wrong — that expression is the newton. It comes from forgetting that work = force × distance multiplies force by an extra length, dropping one factor of m.
D) watt = kg·m²·s⁻² is wrong — that expression is the joule. It comes from forgetting that power = energy ÷ time, which should add one more factor of s⁻¹ (correct watt = kg·m²·s⁻³).
E) coulomb = A·s⁻¹ is wrong — charge = current × time = A·s, not A/s. It comes from inverting the time dependence.

Only pascal is decomposed correctly, so C is the answer.

stem: A lander drops a small test mass and then launches it straight up from the surface of an unfamiliar moon, where the local free-fall acceleration g is unknown and air resistance is negligible. An onboard sensor records the mass's vertical velocity (positive upward) versus time after launch; the recorded data lie on the straight line shown, with two logged points marked. Using the graph, determine the time after launch at which the mass reaches its maximum height.
explanation: The mass is at maximum height when its vertical velocity is zero. Because g is unknown, it must be read as the slope of the v–t line, not assumed. From the two logged points (0 s, 30 m/s) and (3 s, 18 m/s): slope = (18 − 30)/(3 − 0) = −4 m/s², so g = 4 m/s² and the launch speed is v₀ = 30 m/s. Time to v = 0: t = v₀/g = 30/4 = 7.5 s (option C — the line crosses the time axis between the 6 s and 8 s gridlines, confirming this). Traps: A (3.1 s) assumes Earth's g = 9.8 m/s² (30/9.8) instead of reading the slope from the figure. B (4.5 s) uses the interior logged velocity 18 m/s as if it were the launch speed (18/4). D (3.0 s) simply reads off the time-coordinate of the last logged data point, mistaking a plotted point for the apex. E (15 s) computes the total flight time 2v₀/g, confusing the moment of maximum height with the return to the surface.

stem: The graph shows how the force F exerted by two ideal springs, S and T, varies with the distance x by which each spring is compressed. Both springs are compressed until each pushes back with the same force, marked by the horizontal dashed line. Comparing the two springs at this equal force, which one stores the greater elastic potential energy, and by how much?
choices: Both springs store the same energy, because they push back with the same force.
