Spring S, by 0.30 J, because its steeper line means it is the stiffer spring.
explanation: The elastic potential energy stored is the AREA under the force–displacement line, i.e. the area of the triangle from the origit to the compression point: E = ½·F·x. Reading the graph at the dashed equal-force line F = 6.0 N: the steeper spring S reaches that force at x = 0.10 m, while the shallower spring T reaches it only at x = 0.20 m. So E_S = ½·(6.0)(0.10) = 0.30 J and E_T = ½·(6.0)(0.20) = 0.60 J. Spring T stores 0.30 J MORE. The key insight is counter-intuitive: at equal force, the SOFTER spring (smaller slope k) must be compressed farther, enclosing the larger triangle, so it stores more energy. Trap A: assumes energy is fixed by force alone, ignoring that energy is an area that also depends on displacement (equivalently, using E = ½kx gives equal values by forgetting to square x). Trap B: the classic 'stiffer spring stores more' misconception — it computes the correct magnitude 0.30 J but assigns it to the wrong spring by trusting steepness instead of area. Trap D: correct spring and direction, but treats the area as a rectangle F·x instead of the triangle ½·F·x, giving a difference of 1.20 − 0.60 = 0.60 J. Trap E: combines both errors — the 'stiffer stores more' misconception AND the missing ½ factor.

stem: The free-body diagram shows every force acting on a crate as it slides across a rough, horizontal floor. The crate's mass is not stated directly. Using g = 10 m/s², what is the magnitude of the crate's acceleration?
explanation: The figure supplies all data; the text alone is unsolvable. Read the horizontal vectors: applied force F = 48 N (right) and friction f = 18 N (left), so the net horizontal force is F_net = 48 − 18 = 30 N. The mass is never given, so it must come from the weight vector: W = mg gives m = 150/10 = 15 kg. Then a = F_net/m = 30/15 = 2.0 m/s² (A). Distractor traps: B (3.2 = 48/15) ignores friction and uses only the applied force as the net force. C (0.2 = 30/150) uses the weight value 150 N directly as the mass, skipping the W = mg conversion. D (4.4 = 66/15) adds the two horizontal forces (48 + 18) instead of subtracting, mistaking friction as helping the motion. E (1.2 = 18/15) treats the friction magnitude itself as the net driving force. The vertical vectors N and W are equal and cancel vertically; W's only role is to yield the mass, which students who fixate on the horizontal forces overlook.

stem: A tower crane lifts a steel beam vertically at constant speed. The instantaneous mechanical power supplied by the motor can be written as the product of the upward force on the beam and the beam's velocity. Working purely from this relationship, and expressing every quantity in the SI base units kilogram (kg), metre (m) and second (s), which combination is equivalent to the SI unit of this power?
explanation: Power = force × velocity. Force (a newton) in base units is kg·m·s⁻² (from mass × acceleration), and velocity is m·s⁻¹. Multiplying: (kg·m·s⁻²)(m·s⁻¹) = kg·m²·s⁻³, which is the watt. A is correct. B (kg·m²·s⁻²) is the joule: the trap of multiplying force by a distance (m) instead of a velocity (m·s⁻¹), i.e. computing work/energy and forgetting the 'per unit time' that distinguishes power from energy. C (kg·m·s⁻²) is the newton: stopping at the force and forgetting to multiply by velocity at all. D (kg·m·s⁻³) comes from multiplying the newton by a frequency (s⁻¹) instead of a velocity — knowing an extra factor of 'per second' is needed but dropping the length dimension that velocity carries. E (kg·m³·s⁻⁴) comes from using v² instead of v, contaminating the expression with the velocity-squared factor from kinetic energy. Only A results from correctly combining force = kg·m·s⁻² with velocity = m·s⁻¹.

stem: A winch raises a leaky bucket straight up out of a deep well at a constant slow speed. Water drains steadily through a small hole in the bottom, so the bucket grows lighter as it climbs. Because the bucket moves at constant velocity, at every height the rope tension equals the instantaneous weight of the bucket and its remaining water. The graph shows the rope tension T as a function of the height h through which the bucket has been raised. What is the total work done by the rope on the bucket over the entire lift shown?
explanation: Because the bucket rises at constant velocity, the rope tension equals the (changing) weight at every height, so the work the rope does equals the area under the T-vs-h line. Reading the graph, T falls linearly from 150 N at h = 0 to 50 N at h = 8 m. The area is a trapezoid: W = ½(T_start + T_end)·h = ½(150 + 50)(8) = 800 J — equivalently the average tension (100 N) times 8 m. This is answer C. Distractor D (1200 J) assumes the weight stays at its initial 150 N for the whole climb (150 × 8), a rectangle at the top instead of the true trapezoid. Distractor A (400 J) makes the opposite error, using the final 50 N throughout (50 × 8), a rectangle at the bottom. Distractor B (600 J) misreads the line as falling all the way to zero and takes a triangle ½·150·8, ignoring the 50 N floor at the top. Distractor E (1600 J) adds the two endpoint rectangles (150·8 + 50·8) instead of averaging them, double-counting the area. Only the trapezoidal area under the curve gives the correct energy transfer.

stem: A 2.0 kg block slides along a frictionless track. The energy bar chart shows the block's kinetic energy (KE) at three positions A, B and C; the dashed line marks the constant total mechanical energy of the block. Using the chart and taking g = 10 m/s², what is the height of the block above the lowest point of the track at position C?
explanation: The dashed line fixes total mechanical energy at 100 J. From the chart, KE at C = 85 J, so the gravitational PE at C = 100 − 85 = 15 J. Inverting PE = mgh gives h = PE/(mg) = 15/(2.0 × 10) = 0.75 m → A. Distractor B (1.5 m) divides PE by g alone, dropping the mass (h = 15/10). Distractor C (4.25 m) mistakes the labelled KE segment (85 J) for the potential energy and computes 85/(mg) — the classic PE/KE swap. Distractor D (5.0 m) treats the entire 100 J total as potential energy (ignoring that the block is moving at C), giving 100/(mg). Distractor E (7.5 m) uses the correct PE = 15 J but divides by mass only (15/2), forgetting the factor g. Each wrong option maps to one specific error: dropping m, swapping KE for PE, ignoring KE, or dropping g.

stem: Two carts travel on a straight frictionless track. As shown in the diagram, they approach each other, collide, and lock together so that afterward they move as a single body. Using only the masses and velocities given in the figure, what is the velocity of the coupled carts immediately after the collision? (Take "to the right" as positive.)
explanation: The carts move in opposite directions, so their momenta carry opposite signs (this must be read from the figure). Cart 1: p1 = (1.5 kg)(+8 m/s) = +12 kg·m/s. Cart 2: p2 = (2.5 kg)(-2 m/s) = -5 kg·m/s. Total momentum = +7 kg·m/s. Coupled mass = 1.5 + 2.5 = 4.0 kg, so vf = +7/4.0 = +1.75 m/s, i.e. 1.75 m/s to the right (correct: A). Distractor traps: B (4.25) ignores that cart 2 moves the opposite way and adds the momentum magnitudes, (12+5)/4. C (3.0) averages the two velocities (8 and -2) as (8-2)/2, ignoring the mass weighting entirely. D (1.75 left) gets the correct magnitude but assumes the heavier cart (2.5 kg) dictates the final direction; in fact the lighter, faster cart carries more momentum, so the net is to the right. E (7.0) reports the total momentum (7 kg·m/s) as if it were a velocity, forgetting to divide by the combined mass.

stem: A physicist studies gravity aboard a research station where an elevator travels straight upward. Inside the elevator, a small block hangs from a spring scale that is fixed to the elevator's ceiling. The spring-scale reading, the block's mass, and the elevator's velocity–time graph during the measurement are all shown in the figure. Using only this information, determine the gravitational field strength g at the station.
explanation:
The figure supplies three essential quantities: mass m = 6.0 kg, spring-scale reading (the tension/apparent weight) S = 60 N, and the elevator's acceleration, which is the SLOPE of the v–t graph = (8 m/s)/(4 s) = 2.0 m/s² directed upward. Free-body analysis of the block: tension up, weight mg down, with net upward acceleration a. Newton's second law: S − mg = ma, so S = m(g + a), giving g = S/m − a = 60/6 − 2.0 = 10 − 2.0 = 8.0 m/s². Correct = B.

Distractor traps:
A) 2.0 m/s² — graph misreading: the student takes the graph's final VELOCITY value (8 m/s) as if it were the acceleration and computes g = S/m − 8 = 10 − 8 = 2.0, confusing a velocity reading with a slope.
C) 9.8 m/s² — the "assume Earth" trap: the student ignores the figure's data entirely and defaults to Earth's gravitational field strength.
D) 10.0 m/s² — the source's naive one-step error: the elevator's acceleration is ignored and the 60 N reading is treated as the block's true weight, giving g = W/m = 60/6 = 10. (The scale reads apparent weight, not true weight, because the frame accelerates.)
E) 12.0 m/s² — sign error: the student assumes upward acceleration LIGHTENS the reading and writes S = m(g − a), yielding g = S/m + a = 10 + 2.0 = 12.0. This has the direction of the pseudo-effect backwards.

The item is unsolvable from the text alone (no numbers appear in the stem) and requires combining v–t graph interpretation with Newton's second law in an accelerating frame to solve W = mg for g — a genuinely multi-step, figure-essential task rather than a one-step recall plug-in.

stem: A resistor carries a steady current for a time interval t. During this interval the current is I, the potential difference across the resistor is V, its resistance is R, and the total charge that passes through it is Q. A student wants to write an expression for the total electrical energy dissipated in the resistor. Using only dimensional consistency (recall that R = V/I and Q = I·t), four of the five expressions below reduce to the SI unit of energy, the joule. Which expression CANNOT represent an energy?
explanation:
Reduce every expression to SI base units, substituting the unit of resistance Ω = V/A (from R = V/I) and the unit of charge C = A·s (from Q = I·t). The unit of energy is J = V·A·s (since W = V·A and J = W·s).

Correct answer D (V·I): V·A = W = the watt, which is POWER, not energy. It is missing a factor of time (energy = power × time). A student who conflates power with energy — the central misconception this item targets — fails to notice that V·I alone has no time factor and so cannot be a joule.

Why each of the others IS an energy (i.e. why they are wrong choices):
- A (I²·R·t): A²·(V/A)·s = V·A·s = J. This is Joule's heating law; a student who doesn't recognize it may wrongly think squaring the current breaks the units and pick A.
- B (V·Q): V·(A·s) = V·A·s = J. This is W = qV. A student who confuses charge Q with current I would read this as V·I = power and wrongly reject it.
- C (Q²·R / t): (A·s)²·(V/A)/s = A²s²·V/A/s = V·A·s = J. This is the least familiar form; a student who cannot substitute Q = I·t and Ω = V/A wrongly discards it as the "odd" expression.
- E (V²·t / R): V²·s·(A/V) = V·A·s = J. A student who mishandles the division by R (e.g. multiplies instead) may wrongly reject it.

Each distractor is a genuine energy expression that a specific reasoning error would cause a student to select instead of D; D is the unique expression whose dimensions are power, so exactly one option is correct and none is trivially eliminable without carrying out the base-unit reduction.

stem: While studying a rubber ball bouncing off a rigid wall, a student wants to build a "characteristic number" — a pure (dimensionless) quantity whose value does not change if the unit system is switched from SI to any other consistent system. From the collision the student can measure six quantities: the impulse J delivered by the wall, the ball's momentum p, the average force F exerted during contact, the power P developed during contact, the work W done by the wall on the ball, and the ball's kinetic energy K. Expressing each ratio below in base dimensions (M, L, T), which ONE is dimensionless?
explanation:
Reduce each quantity to base dimensions. Force [F] = M L T⁻²; momentum [p] = M L T⁻¹; impulse [J] = [F][t] = M L T⁻¹; work/energy [W] = [K] = M L² T⁻²; power [P] = M L² T⁻³.

A (correct): [J]/[p] = (M L T⁻¹)/(M L T⁻¹) = 1. Impulse and momentum are LIKE quantities (impulse is precisely a change of momentum), so their ratio is a pure number — dimension 1 — exactly the "ratio of like quantities is dimensionless" idea.

B (trap — velocity): [P]/[F] = (M L² T⁻³)/(M L T⁻²) = L T⁻¹. Misconception: treating power and force as the same "kind" of quantity because both describe the wall's push; this leaves a residual velocity, not 1.

C (trap — inverse time): [F]/[p] = (M L T⁻²)/(M L T⁻¹) = T⁻¹. Misconception: regarding force and momentum as interchangeable "measures of motion"; but force is the time-rate of momentum, so a factor T⁻¹ survives.

D (trap — time): [K]/[P] = (M L² T⁻²)/(M L² T⁻³) = T. Misconception: energy and power look like the "same energy quantity," yet power carries an extra T⁻¹, leaving a residual time.

E (trap — length): [W]/[F] = (M L² T⁻²)/(M L T⁻²) = L. Misconception: since W = F·d, the student assumes the ratio cancels both; it actually returns the displacement (length).

Only J/p is a ratio of two quantities with identical dimensions, so it alone is dimensionless.

stem: The diagram shows a hydraulic jack in cross-section. A worker presses straight down with force F₁ on the far end of a rigid lever that pivots at point P; the lever drives a small piston down into an incompressible, oil-filled chamber. The oil transmits the pressure to a large piston, which pushes upward on a load. The lever and both pistons are weightless and all friction is negligible. Using only the dimensions labelled in the figure, what is the magnitude of the upward force F₂ that the large piston exerts on the load?
explanation:
Two syllabus concepts must be chained, and every number lives in the figure. Step 1 (lever / moments): balancing torques about pivot P, the force delivered to the small piston is F_p = F₁ × (effort arm / piston arm) = 40 N × (45 cm / 9 cm) = 40 × 5 = 200 N. Step 2 (Pascal's principle with circular pistons): the pressure F_p/A₁ is transmitted undiminished, so F₂ = F_p × A₂/A₁. Because area ∝ diameter², A₂/A₁ = (d₂/d₁)² = (12 cm / 3 cm)² = 4² = 16. Thus F₂ = 200 N × 16 = 3200 N (D).

Distractor traps:
A) 160 N = 40 × 4 — ignores the lever entirely AND uses the linear diameter ratio (4) instead of its square (forgets area ∝ d²): both key errors at once.
B) 640 N = 40 × 16 — applies Pascal correctly (area ratio 16) but forgets the lever, feeding the raw 40 N into the fluid instead of the amplified 200 N.
C) 800 N = 200 × 4 — includes the lever correctly (200 N) but scales force by the diameter ratio (4) rather than the area ratio (16), the classic 'forgot to square' misconception.
E) 16 000 N = 40 × 5² × 4² — squares the lever-arm ratio as well as the diameter ratio, wrongly treating the lever like a second area amplification (25 × 16 × 40).
Only D uses moments once (linearly) and Pascal's law with the squared area ratio.

stem: A student places an empty graduated cylinder on an electronic balance and, without taring it, slowly pours a liquid in, recording the balance's total reading against the liquid volume. The resulting data fall on the straight line shown. What is the density of the liquid?
explanation: The balance reads cylinder + liquid, so the plotted mass is offset by the empty cylinder's mass. The line does not pass through the origin: its y-intercept (0, 50) is the empty-cylinder mass (the untared tare). Density is the mass of liquid per unit volume, which is the SLOPE of the line, not the ratio at any single point. Slope = Δm/ΔV = (130 − 50)/(100 − 0) = 80/100 = 0.80 g/cm³ (A). B (1.30) takes one point's total mass over its volume, 130 g ÷ 100 cm³, ignoring that 50 g of that reading is the cylinder — the giveaway is that this ratio changes from point to point, so it cannot be a density. C (1.25) inverts the relation, computing V/m = 100 ÷ 80 (specific volume, cm³/g) instead of m/V. D (0.50) misreads the graph: it reads the y-intercept 50 g and divides by 100 cm³, treating the offset itself as the density. E (1.60) correctly subtracts the 50 g tare to get 80 g of liquid but pairs it with the wrong volume (50 cm³ instead of 100 cm³), a point-mismatch error. Only the slope, computed from two points with the intercept accounted for, gives the true density.

stem: A rigid rectangular block is clamped so that it stays completely submerged and motionless, straddling the sharp boundary between a layer of oil (on top) and water (below), exactly as shown in the figure. The block's uniform horizontal cross-sectional area is A = 200 cm², and the portions of the block sitting in each fluid are marked on the figure. Using g = 10 m/s², what is the total buoyant force the fluids exert on the block?
explanation: Archimedes' principle applied to each fluid layer separately: buoyant force equals the total weight of displaced fluid, and each layer contributes according to the volume of block it surrounds. From the figure, 9 cm of the block's height is in oil and 6 cm is in water, with A = 200 cm² = 0.02 m². Oil part: V = 0.02 × 0.09 = 1.8×10⁻³ m³ → F = 750 × 1.8e-3 × 10 = 13.5 N. Water part: V = 0.02 × 0.06 = 1.2×10⁻³ m³ → F = 1000 × 1.2e-3 × 10 = 12.0 N. Total = 25.5 N (C). Trap A (22.5 N): treats the whole 15 cm as if immersed in oil only, ignoring the denser water layer. Trap B (24.0 N): uses the block's weight, mass × g = 2.4 × 10, wrongly assuming buoyancy depends on the object's mass — buoyancy depends only on displaced fluid, so the mass is irrelevant. Trap D (27.0 N): reads the figure inverted, assigning water density to the upper portion and oil density to the lower portion (1000×1.8e-3×10 + 750×1.2e-3×10). Trap E (30.0 N): treats the whole 15 cm as if immersed in water only, ignoring the lighter oil layer.

stem: The figure (top view) shows water flowing steadily through a horizontal pipe. A single wide inlet divides into two identical narrow outlet branches. Using only the cross-sectional areas and the inlet speed marked in the figure, what is the speed of the water in each narrow branch?
explanation:
Volumetric flow rate is conserved and, because the two outlet branches are identical, the incoming flow splits equally between them: A₁v₁ = 2·A₂v₂. From the figure, Q_in = A₁v₁ = 6.0 cm² × 4.0 m/s = 24 (cm²·m/s). Each branch therefore carries 24/2 = 12, so v₂ = 12 / A₂ = 12 / 2.0 = 6.0 m/s → C.
Distractor traps: A) 1.3 m/s inverts the continuity relation, taking v₂ = v₁·A₂/A₁ = 4.0×2.0/6.0 (speed treated as proportional to area) and ignores the split. B) 2.0 m/s assumes the SPEED itself halves at the junction (v₁/2), confusing division of the flow with division of the velocity. D) 12 m/s applies single-pipe continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, forgetting that the flow divides between two branches (this is the speed you would get in ONE branch if it carried all the flow). E) 24 m/s multiplies by the branch count instead of dividing, taking v₂ = 2·A₁v₁/A₂, i.e. assuming more branches make the water proportionally faster. Each value comes from a distinct, specific error; only the equal-split continuity path gives 6.0 m/s.

stem: Two carts sit on a straight, frictionless horizontal track. The BEFORE panel of the figure shows cart P moving toward cart Q, which is stationary; the AFTER panel shows both carts once the collision is over. The collision is perfectly elastic, and no external horizontal forces act. Using the masses and initial velocity given in the figure, what is the velocity of cart P immediately after the collision?
choices: 3 m/s to the left (P rebounds backward)
3 m/s to the right (P continues forward)
6 m/s to the right (P is unaffected)
6 m/s to the left (P rebounds at its original speed)
explanation: The figure supplies the essential data: cart P has mass 1 kg moving right at 6 m/s, cart Q has mass 3 kg at rest. For a 1D elastic collision, momentum is conserved (m_P v_P = m_P v_P' + m_Q v_Q') and, because kinetic energy is also conserved, the relative velocity reverses (v_P − v_Q = −(v_P' − v_Q'), i.e. v_P + v_P' = v_Q'). Substituting v_Q' = 6 + v_P' into 6 = v_P' + 3v_Q' gives 6 = v_P' + 3(6 + v_P') = 4v_P' + 18, so v_P' = −3 m/s: cart P rebounds at 3 m/s to the LEFT (and v_Q' = +3 m/s). Correct answer A. Distractor B (0 m/s) is the equal-mass velocity-exchange result misapplied here — P would stop ONLY if the masses were equal, but Q is heavier, so P must bounce back. C (3 m/s right) has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign, from treating P as passing through rather than reflecting off the heavier cart. D (6 m/s right) assumes the collision leaves P unchanged, ignoring momentum transfer entirely. E (6 m/s left) is the m_Q ≫ m_P limit (a bounce off an effectively immovable wall), which overstates Q's mass; since m_Q is only 3× m_P, the rebound speed is 3 m/s, not the full 6 m/s. Every distractor requires the figure's mass values to evaluate, so the item cannot be answered from the text alone.

stem: A solid rectangular block is held fully submerged and at rest in a fluid of density rho = 1000 kg/m^3 (take g = 10 m/s^2). The pressure the fluid exerts on each face is shown by the arrows in the diagram (arrow length is proportional to pressure magnitude). Reading the depth of the block's top face, the depth of its bottom face, and the area of each horizontal face from the figure, what is the NET UPWARD force that the fluid pressure exerts on the block?
explanation: The net upward thrust comes only from the difference in hydrostatic pressure between the bottom and top horizontal faces (the horizontal forces on the vertical side faces cancel). From the figure, h_top = 0.30 m, h_bottom = 0.50 m, and each horizontal face area A = 0.10 m^2. Net force = (P_bottom - P_top)*A = rho*g*(h_bottom - h_top)*A = 1000*10*(0.50 - 0.30)*0.10 = 200 N (which equals rho*g*V of the displaced fluid). Correct: B. Traps: A = 0 N assumes that because pressure acts equally in all directions it must produce no net force (ignores that pressure grows with depth, so the bottom is pushed up harder than the top is pushed down). C = 400 N uses the pressure at the block's mid-depth (0.40 m) times one face area, treating buoyancy as centroid-pressure*area instead of the top-to-bottom difference. D = 500 N counts only the upward force on the bottom face (rho*g*h_bottom*A) and forgets to subtract the downward force on the top face. E = 800 N adds the magnitudes of the bottom-face and top-face forces, rho*g*(h_bottom + h_top)*A, instead of subtracting them.

stem: A student measures the specific heat capacity of an unknown metal. A small electric immersion heater rated at 60 W is embedded in a 0.50 kg block of the metal, which is well insulated so that essentially all the electrical energy is absorbed by the block. When the heater is switched on for 5.0 minutes, the block's temperature rises steadily from 20 °C to 80 °C. What value should the student report for the specific heat capacity of the metal?
explanation: The heat supplied is the electrical energy delivered: Q = P·t = 60 W × (5.0 × 60 s) = 60 × 300 = 18000 J. The temperature change is ΔT = 80 − 20 = 60 °C, and m = 0.50 kg. Rearranging the sensible-heat relation Q = mcΔT gives c = Q/(mΔT) = 18000/(0.50 × 60) = 600 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (A). Distractor traps: (B) 450 uses the FINAL temperature 80 °C in place of the temperature CHANGE, computing 18000/(0.50 × 80) — confusing T with ΔT. (C) 300 OMITS the mass, dividing the energy by ΔT alone: 18000/60. (D) 108 converts the temperature difference to kelvin by ADDING 273 (ΔT → 60 + 273 = 333), a misconception that an interval must be shifted like an absolute temperature: 18000/(0.50 × 333) ≈ 108. (E) 10 fails to convert the 5.0 minutes to seconds, using t = 5 so Q = 60 × 5 = 300 J and c = 300/(0.50 × 60). Each wrong option isolates one specific error; only A applies every step correctly.

stem:
A fixed quantity of ideal gas is carried once around a closed cycle made of three steps and returns exactly to its starting state A:

• Step 1 (A → B): the gas absorbs 600 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings.
• Step 2 (B → C): the volume is held fixed while the gas releases 500 J of heat.
• Step 3 (C → A): the gas is compressed, the surroundings doing 300 J of work on it, bringing the gas back to state A.

Using the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = Q − W, with W the work done by the gas), what is the heat exchanged by the gas during Step 3?
choices: The gas absorbs 100 J of heat.
The gas releases 200 J of heat.
The gas absorbs 400 J of heat.
The gas releases 300 J of heat.
It cannot be determined without knowing the pressures and volumes at A, B and C.
explanation:
Because internal energy is a state function and the gas returns to state A, the total change over the cycle is zero: ΔU₁ + ΔU₂ + ΔU₃ = 0.
Step 1: ΔU₁ = Q − W = 600 − 200 = +400 J.
Step 2 (isochoric, W = 0): ΔU₂ = −500 − 0 = −500 J.
Cycle closure: ΔU₃ = −(400 − 500) = +100 J.
Step 3: work done BY the gas is W = −300 J (the surroundings do +300 J on it during compression). First law: Q₃ = ΔU₃ + W = 100 + (−300) = −200 J, i.e. the gas RELEASES 200 J. Correct = B.

Trap analysis:
A (absorbs 100 J): correctly finds ΔU₃ = +100 J but drops the work term, setting Q = ΔU — ignoring that compression work must be accounted for.
C (absorbs 400 J): sign error on the work — treats the 300 J compression as work done BY the gas (+300), giving Q = 100 + 300 = +400 J absorbed.
D (releases 300 J): conflates heat with work, reporting the compression work itself as the heat and ignoring ΔU₃ entirely.
E (cannot be determined): the misconception that first-law energy accounting requires the full P–V path/state variables, whereas ΔU is path-independent and the given heats and works are sufficient.

stem: Two identical hot copper blocks are each suspended by a thin insulating thread so that almost no heat can escape along the thread. Block 1 hangs in an ordinary room full of air at 20 °C. Block 2 hangs inside a sealed chamber whose walls are also at 20 °C, but the chamber has been pumped down to a hard vacuum. Both blocks are eventually observed to cool down to 20 °C. Which statement correctly describes how Block 2 loses its heat and how its cooling compares with Block 1's?
choices: Block 2 cannot cool at all: with no surrounding matter there is no path for heat to leave, so it stays hot indefinitely.
Block 2 cools mainly by convection of the tiny amount of gas left in the chamber, at essentially the same rate as Block 1.
Block 2 cools by conduction straight across the empty gap to the chamber walls, since conduction can still carry heat through empty space.

Block 2 cools by emitting thermal (electromagnetic) radiation to the walls — the only mode needing no medium — and cools more slowly than Block 1 because conduction and convection through air are now absent.
Block 2 cools faster than Block 1, because removing the air lets radiation travel more strongly and so carries heat away more quickly.
explanation: The key idea is that conduction and convection both require a material medium, while radiation transports energy by electromagnetic waves and therefore crosses a vacuum. In the evacuated chamber there is essentially no matter to support conduction or convection, so the only remaining mechanism is thermal radiation to the cooler walls — hence Block 2 does cool, but with fewer active mechanisms it cools more slowly than the air-surrounded Block 1. (D) captures both the mode and the correct rate comparison. Trap in (A): the misconception that every heat-transfer mode needs matter, so a vacuum must trap all heat — it ignores radiation. Trap in (B): treats the residual gas as still enabling ordinary convection at a normal rate; a hard vacuum has far too little matter for meaningful convection. Trap in (C): claims conduction can occur across empty space, but conduction needs a continuous material medium. Trap in (E): assumes a vacuum boosts radiation; the radiated power depends on the block's temperature and emissivity, not on the presence of air, and removing air only removes extra cooling paths, so Block 2 must cool slower, not faster.

stem: Three small charged spheres are fixed on the coordinate grid shown, where each grid square represents 10 cm. The central sphere q₀ experiences electrostatic forces from the other two charges (the two force arrows F₁ and F₂ are indicated). Using Coulomb's constant k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C², determine the magnitude of the net electrostatic force acting on q₀.
explanation: Read from the figure: q₀ = +2 μC at the origin, q₁ = +20 μC at 30 cm along +x, and q₂ = −15 μC at 30 cm along +y (each square = 10 cm, so both distances r = 0.30 m). Force from q₁: F₁ = k|q₀q₁|/r² = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁶)(20×10⁻⁶)/(0.30)² = 0.36/0.09 = 4 N; both charges positive, so it is repulsive and points in the −x direction (as the F₁ arrow shows). Force from q₂: F₂ = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁶)(15×10⁻⁶)/(0.30)² = 0.27/0.09 = 3 N; opposite signs, so it is attractive and points toward q₂ in the +y direction. The two forces are perpendicular, so the net magnitude is √(4²+3²) = 5 N (C). Trap A (1 N): treats the two forces as collinear and opposing, computing 4−3. Trap B (1.5 N): uses Coulomb's law with 1/r instead of 1/r², ignoring the inverse-square dependence (F₁=1.2 N, F₂=0.9 N, net √(1.2²+0.9²)=1.5 N) — the core misconception this item targets. Trap D (7 N): adds the magnitudes as scalars (4+3), ignoring that the forces act along perpendicular directions. Trap E (25 N): correctly forms 4²+3² but forgets to take the square root.

stem: A technician measures the circuit shown, powered by an ideal 12 V source with no internal resistance. Resistor R1 is wired in series with a parallel pair, R2 and R3. Using the resistance values printed on the schematic, what total current does the source deliver?
explanation: The parallel pair combines as R_p = (R2·R3)/(R2+R3) = (6·3)/(6+3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Adding the series resistor: R_total = R1 + R_p = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω. Ohm's law for the whole loop: I = ε/R_total = 12/6 = 2.0 A → B. Distractor traps: A (0.92 A) treats the two parallel resistors as if they were also in series, using R = 4+6+3 = 13 Ω. C (2.7 A) forgets the final reciprocal step in the parallel formula — it computes 1/R2 + 1/R3 = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 and uses 0.5 Ω directly, giving R = 4.5 Ω. D (3.0 A) ignores the parallel branch entirely and divides by R1 alone (12/4). E (6.0 A) ignores the series resistor R1 and divides by the parallel equivalent alone (12/2). Each wrong option corresponds to one specific structural misreading of the network, so the figure — not the text — must be interpreted to get the topology right.

stem: A lithium battery for an electric scooter is labelled with a capacity of "10 A·h" (ampere-hours). A student wants to understand what this rating actually measures. Reasoning only from the units — an ampere-hour is an ampere multiplied by an hour, i.e. an electric current multiplied by a time — which physical quantity does the ampere-hour measure, and what is the corresponding coherent SI unit?
explanation: Dimensional reasoning: an ampere-hour is (current)×(time). Since electric charge is defined as charge = current × time, any unit of the form (current unit)×(time unit) must measure charge. The coherent SI unit of charge is the coulomb, where 1 C = 1 A·s; thus 1 A·h = 3600 C. So the ampere-hour rates the total charge the battery can deliver, and the answer is A. Trap in B (ampere): reading the "ampere" inside "ampere-hour" and ignoring that it is multiplied by a time, which downgrades the quantity from current×time back to just current. Trap in C (joule): confusing charge capacity with energy capacity — energy would require multiplying by a voltage (giving watt-hours, W·h, = J), a very common real-world mix-up, but A·h alone has no volt factor. Trap in D (volt): associating a battery only with its voltage rating; the volt is joule per coulomb, not current×time. Trap in E (watt): confusing a stored total (capacity) with a rate of delivery — the watt is a power (energy per time), which has an extra 1/time compared with the charge dimension.

stem: The circuit shown is powered by an ideal battery with no internal resistance. Between junctions A and B the network divides, and additional resistors lie in the main loop with the source. Using ONLY the component values marked in the schematic, determine the total current I that the battery delivers to the network.
explanation:
Reduce the network step by step. Each parallel branch between A and B is itself two series resistors: upper branch R2+R3 = 8+4 = 12 Ω, lower branch R4+R5 = 2+4 = 6 Ω. Combine the two branches in parallel: (12·6)/(12+6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. This 4 Ω block is in series with R1 = 1 Ω and R6 = 1 Ω in the main loop, so R_total = 1+4+1 = 6 Ω. Ohm's law gives I = V/R_total = 24/6 = 4.0 A (C).

Distractor traps:
A) 1.2 A — treats every resistor as one big series loop (1+8+4+2+4+1 = 20 Ω); fails to recognize the two branches are in parallel.
B) 3.0 A — recognizes a parallel section but mis-reduces it to a single 6 Ω branch instead of 4 Ω (24/(1+6+1)); forgets that an equivalent parallel resistance is smaller than either branch.
D) 4.8 A — reduces correctly to the 4 Ω block and adds R1 but omits the second series resistor R6 (24/(1+4)); overlooks one series element in the loop.
E) 6.0 A — uses the parallel block alone (24/4), ignoring that the series resistors R1 and R6 also limit the current.

stem: In the circuit shown, a battery drives a steady current through a single resistor R. A voltmeter measures the potential difference across R and an ammeter measures the current through it; both readings are given in the figure. Using these readings, determine the resistance R and then express the SI unit of that resistance entirely in terms of the SI base units (kg, m, s, A). Which single option states BOTH correctly?
explanation: Reading the figure: V = 9.0 V across R and I = 3.0 mA = 3.0×10⁻³ A through it. Ohm's law gives R = V/I = 9.0 / 3.0×10⁻³ = 3000 Ω = 3.0 kΩ. To express the ohm in base units, start from the volt: 1 V = 1 J/C = (kg·m²·s⁻²)/(A·s) = kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹. Then 1 Ω = 1 V/A = kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻². Option A has both the value and the base-unit derivation right. B keeps the correct value but gives the base units of the VOLT (kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹) — it forgets the extra division by the ampere when going from V to Ω. C keeps the correct value but has an s⁻² instead of s⁻³, the trap of treating the volt like an energy (joule ∝ s⁻²) and dropping the per-second from power. D uses the correct base units but computes R = V·I = 9.0 × 3.0×10⁻³ = 0.027 Ω = 27 mΩ, multiplying instead of dividing. E uses the correct base units but inverts the ratio, taking I/V (a conductance) and reporting it as ≈333 Ω = 0.33 kΩ. Only A is fully correct.

stem: In a calibration chamber, a small charged bead carrying q = +5.0 µC drifts through a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B = 0.30 T. The figure shows, in the plane of the page, the bead's velocity vector v (speed v = 4.0×10⁴ m/s) and the field direction (the ⊙ symbols mean B points straight out of the page). The velocity is perpendicular to B. Using the directions given in the figure, determine the magnitude AND direction of the magnetic force on the bead at the instant shown.
choices: 0.060 N, directed toward the bottom of the page
0.060 N, directed toward the top of the page
0.060 N, directed to the left (opposite to v)
0.060 N, directed out of the page (along B)
0.20 N, directed toward the bottom of the page
explanation: Magnitude: F = qvB = (5.0×10⁻⁶ C)(4.0×10⁴ m/s)(0.30 T) = 0.060 N. Direction: F = qv×B. From the figure v points right (+x) and B points out of the page (+z); x̂×ẑ = −ŷ, and since q is positive the force is along −ŷ, i.e. toward the bottom of the page — so A is correct. B keeps the right magnitude but reverses the right-hand rule (or treats the charge as negative), giving "up." C assumes the magnetic force opposes the velocity like a drag/friction force (it is actually perpendicular to v). D places the force along B itself, ignoring that v×B is perpendicular to both v and B. E has the correct downward direction but drops the factor B and computes F = qv = 0.20 N, a units/formula error. The direction cannot be obtained from the text alone — it requires reading v and B off the figure, so the figure is essential.

stem: A materials student suspends five small, identical spheres — each made of a different pure metal: aluminium, cobalt, copper, iron, and nickel — from light threads so they hang freely. She slowly brings the NORTH pole of a strong bar magnet toward each sphere in turn and records the sideways deflection of its thread. She then repeats the whole test using the SOUTH pole. Which statement correctly describes what she observes?
choices: All five spheres deflect toward the magnet, because any metal is attracted to a sufficiently strong magnet.
The iron, cobalt, and nickel spheres deflect strongly toward the magnet, and each is attracted by either pole; the aluminium and copper spheres barely move.
Only the iron sphere deflects strongly; the cobalt and nickel spheres behave essentially like the aluminium and copper spheres.
The copper sphere deflects strongly because copper's high electrical conductivity makes it magnetic, while iron, cobalt, and nickel stay still.
The iron, cobalt, and nickel spheres are pulled toward the north pole but are pushed away when the south pole is presented.
explanation: Fe, Co, and Ni are the classic ferromagnetic metals: a nearby magnet induces magnetization in them so they are strongly attracted. Because the sphere magnetizes in response to whichever pole approaches, the induced pole is always opposite the approaching pole, so the attraction occurs with EITHER the north or the south pole. Aluminium is only weakly paramagnetic and copper is weakly diamagnetic, so on this macroscopic scale both are effectively non-magnetic and barely move — making B correct. A is the trap that "all metals are magnetic" (only a few ferromagnetic elements are). C is the trap of remembering only iron and forgetting that cobalt and nickel are equally ferromagnetic. D encodes the common conflation of electrical conductivity with magnetism (good conductors like Cu are not ferromagnetic). E is the misconception that magnetic attraction is pole-dependent; in fact induced attraction of a ferromagnet is independent of which pole is presented, so reversing the pole never turns attraction into repulsion.

stem: A flat coil of 50 turns is placed in a changing magnetic field. The graph shows the magnetic flux Φ through a single turn of the coil as a function of time t. Over the interval shown, what is the greatest magnitude of the EMF induced in the coil?
explanation: The induced EMF equals N times the slope of the flux-time graph: EMF = N·|ΔΦ/Δt|. Reading the four straight segments: 0–2 s slope = 0.6/2 = 0.3 Wb/s; 2–4 s slope = 0 (flat); 4–5 s slope = (0.2−0.6)/1 = −0.4 Wb/s; 5–8 s slope = (0.5−0.2)/3 = 0.1 Wb/s. The steepest segment is 4–5 s, so the maximum EMF = 50 × 0.4 = 20 V (C). Distractor traps: (B) 15 V takes the 0–2 s segment (50×0.3), the visually largest rise, failing to compare slope magnitudes and notice the steeper 4–5 s drop. (A) 5 V takes the shallow final 5–8 s segment (50×0.1). (D) 30 V misreads the 4–5 s drop as the full 0.6 Wb height over 1 s (50×0.6) instead of the actual 0.4 Wb change. (E) 3.1 V uses the net change over the whole interval (0.5 Wb over 8 s → 50×0.0625), averaging instead of taking the local rate on the steepest segment.

stem: A single oscillator drives one end of a long string that is made of two firmly joined segments of different mass per unit length. In the first segment the transverse wave travels at 10 m/s and has a wavelength of 0.40 m. When the wave crosses the junction into the second (lighter) segment, its speed increases to 20 m/s. What is the wavelength of the wave in the second segment?
explanation: Key insight: the whole string oscillates at the frequency imposed by the single oscillator, so the FREQUENCY is the same on both sides of the junction; only speed and wavelength change. Step 1 — find the frequency in segment 1: f = v1/λ1 = 10 / 0.40 = 25 Hz. Step 2 — this same 25 Hz applies in segment 2, so λ2 = v2/f = 20 / 25 = 0.80 m (C). Distractor traps: (A) 0.20 m assumes wavelength varies inversely with speed, λ1·(v1/v2) = 0.40·(10/20) — the wrong proportionality direction. (B) 0.40 m assumes the wavelength itself is conserved across the boundary, the core misconception of mistaking which quantity (frequency, not wavelength) stays constant. (D) 1.25 m computes f = 25 Hz correctly but applies the relation inverted, λ = f/v = 25/20. (E) 1.60 m scales the wavelength by the square of the speed ratio, λ1·(v2/v1)² = 0.40·4, over-applying the proportionality. Only C uses the correct conserved quantity and the correct form λ = v/f.

stem: A small cork floats on the surface of a calm lake. As a steady train of water waves passes, the cork bobs vertically up and down. The graph shows the cork's vertical displacement as a function of time. Assuming the waves keep arriving at the same steady rate, how many complete wave crests pass the cork during one full minute?
explanation: From the graph, the cork completes one full up-and-down cycle every 4.0 s, so the period is T = 4.0 s. Each passing crest corresponds to one complete oscillation, so the frequency (crests per second) is f = 1/T = 1/4.0 = 0.25 Hz. In one minute (60 s) the number of crests is f x 60 = 0.25 x 60 = 15 (option C). Each distractor encodes a specific error: (A) 0.25 stops at the frequency in Hz (crests per SECOND) and forgets to convert to per minute. (B) 7.5 misreads the period as 8.0 s by treating the two visible cycles as a single oscillation, giving 60/8. (D) 30 misreads the period as 2.0 s by mistaking the first return to zero displacement (a half-cycle) for a full cycle, giving 60/2 = 30. (E) 240 is the key inverse-relationship trap: it multiplies by the period instead of dividing (60 x T = 60 x 4), i.e. treating a longer period as producing MORE crests — the exact reversal of T = 1/f.

stem: A physics teacher sets up four monochromatic light sources, S1, S2, S3 and S4. She marks the wavelength of each source with a labelled pointer on the visible-spectrum scale shown in the figure. She reminds the class that all four beams travel through the same vacuum at the identical speed c. Using ONLY the wavelength positions read from the figure, which single statement is correct?
choices: S1 emits both the highest-frequency and the highest-energy photons of the four sources.
S4 emits the highest-energy photons, because it sits farthest along the spectrum from the starting edge.
S2 and S3 must emit photons of equal energy, since both are marked in the middle region of the band.
S4 emits the highest-frequency light, because red light has the greatest frequency of all visible colours.
All four sources emit photons of equal energy, because in vacuum every beam moves at the same speed c.
explanation: The figure shows S1 at 440 nm, S2 at 520 nm, S3 at 590 nm and S4 at 660 nm, so S1 has the SHORTEST wavelength. Since f = c/λ, the shortest wavelength gives the highest frequency, and since E = hc/λ (equivalently E = hf), the shortest wavelength also gives the highest photon energy. Both properties therefore belong to S1, making A correct. B encodes the misconception that 'farther along the band = more energy'; in fact S4 (660 nm, red) has the LONGEST wavelength and hence the LOWEST energy. C assumes a middle position means equal energy, but S2 (520 nm) and S3 (590 nm) have different wavelengths and therefore different energies. D is the classic red/violet frequency reversal: red has the LOWEST frequency, not the highest. E confuses wave speed with photon energy: all beams share speed c, but energy depends on frequency/wavelength (E = hc/λ), which differs for each source. Only the figure supplies the wavelengths that fix the ordering, so the item cannot be answered from the text alone.

stem: The ray diagram shows a vertical object arrow placed in front of a concave mirror. The focal point F and the centre of curvature C are marked on the principal axis, and two reflected principal rays are drawn. Each grid square represents 6 cm. Reading the required quantities from the diagram and using the mirror equation together with the magnification relation, determine the height and orientation of the image formed by the reflected rays.
explanation:
Read from the figure: the object stands 6 squares from the mirror vertex, so do = 36 cm; F is 2 squares out, so f = 12 cm (C at 4 squares = 24 cm confirms this, since f = R/2); the object arrow is 1 square tall, so ho = 6 cm. Mirror equation: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/12 − 1/36 = 3/36 − 1/36 = 2/36 = 1/18, giving di = +18 cm (positive ⇒ real image in front of the mirror, exactly where the two reflected rays cross, 3 squares from the vertex). Magnification m = −di/do = −18/36 = −0.5, so hi = m·ho = −0.5 × 6 = −3.0 cm: the image is 3.0 cm tall and inverted (negative sign, rays cross below the axis). Correct answer A.

Distractor traps:
B (6.0 cm, inverted): assumes the image is the same size as the object (m = −1), the misconception that a concave mirror reproduces object size or that the object sits at C; that would only hold if do = 24 cm, but the object is at 36 cm.
C (12.0 cm, inverted): mistakes the centre of curvature for the focal point, using f = 24 cm → 1/di = 1/24 − 1/36 = 1/72, di = 72 cm, m = −2 → magnified; error of reading C as F.
D (3.0 cm, upright): correct magnitude but wrong orientation — treats m as positive and forgets that a real image from a concave mirror (rays crossing below the axis) is inverted.
E (1.5 cm, inverted): sign error in the mirror equation, adding instead of subtracting: 1/di = 1/do + 1/f = 1/36 + 1/12 = 4/36, di = 9 cm, m = −0.25 → 1.5 cm.

stem: A narrow beam of light travels straight down through three stacked, non-mixing transparent layers whose interfaces are horizontal and parallel. The measured path of the beam, the angle it makes with the normal in each layer, and the refractive indices of the upper two layers are shown in the diagram. The refractive index of the bottom layer is unknown. Reading the required quantities from the figure, what is the refractive index of the bottom layer?
explanation: Because the interfaces are parallel, the quantity n·sinθ (the component tied to the horizontal direction) is conserved at every interface: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ = n₃sinθ₃. So the bottom index can be found from ANY layer paired with the bottom layer. Using the air (top) layer read from the figure: n₃ = n₁sinθ₁/sinθ₃ = (1.00)(sin45°)/(sin30°) = 0.707/0.500 = 1.41. Cross-check with the water layer gives (1.33)(sin32°)/(sin30°) ≈ 1.41 — the water data are consistent but not actually needed, which is the key insight. The ray bends toward the normal at each interface (45°→32°→30°), consistent with entering progressively denser media (1.00 < 1.33 < 1.41). Distractor traps: (A) 1.25 swaps the two angles at the bottom interface, computing n₂sinθ₃/sinθ₂ instead of n₂sinθ₂/sinθ₃. (B) 1.33 assumes the bottom index equals the middle (water) index because the ray barely changes direction there (32°→30°) — but any change in angle requires n₃≠n₂. (D) 1.77 wrongly chains the first-interface ratio onto water's index, n₃ = n_water·sin45°/sin32°, mixing angles from different interfaces. (E) 1.88 uses water's index paired with the air angle, n₃ = n_water·sin45°/sin30°, matching the correct index to the wrong layer's angle. Only C respects the conserved quantity n·sinθ.

stem: The figure shows a single ray of light striking a plane mirror at point P. The dashed line is the normal to the mirror at P, and the marked angle is measured between the incident ray and the mirror's surface. The reflected ray is not drawn. Using the law of reflection, what is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
explanation:
The angle marked in the figure (32°) is measured from the MIRROR SURFACE, but the law of reflection uses angles measured from the NORMAL. So the angle of incidence is i = 90° − 32° = 58°. By the law of reflection the angle of reflection equals i = 58°. The incident and reflected rays lie on opposite sides of the normal, each 58° from it, so the total angle between them is 2i = 2 × 58° = 116° (E, correct).

Distractor traps:
A) 32° — reports the labeled surface angle unchanged, ignoring both the normal conversion and the two-ray geometry.
B) 58° — correctly finds the angle of reflection from the normal but stops there, reporting a single ray's angle instead of the separation between the two rays.
C) 64° — treats the marked 32° as the angle of incidence itself (measuring from the surface instead of the normal) and doubles it: 2 × 32°. Encodes the classic "measured from the mirror, not the normal" misconception.
D) 90° — assumes the incident and reflected rays are perpendicular to each other, a fixed-geometry misconception that ignores the actual incidence angle.

The item is figure-essential: the 32° value and its reference (to the surface, not the normal) appear only in the diagram, and the reflected ray is deliberately omitted so it cannot be measured directly.

stem: Two carts, A and B, rest on a horizontal frictionless track. Their masses and their velocities immediately before impact are shown in the figure. The carts then undergo a head-on elastic collision. Taking rightward as the positive direction, what is the velocity of cart A immediately after the collision?
choices: 0 m/s (cart A is momentarily at rest)
explanation: Read from the figure: cart A is 3 kg moving at +4 m/s, cart B is 1 kg moving at -4 m/s (leftward). For a 1D elastic collision, v_A' = [(m_A-m_B)/(m_A+m_B)]v_A + [2m_B/(m_A+m_B)]v_B = [(3-1)/4](4) + [2/4](-4) = 2 - 2 = 0 m/s. Check: momentum before = 3(4)+1(-4)=8; after = 3(0)+1(+8)=8; KE before = 24+8=32 J, after = 0+32=32 J — both conserved, so cart A is momentarily at rest while cart B leaves at +8 m/s. Trap A (+4): student ignores the direction of B's velocity, plugging v_B=+4 to get 2+2=4 m/s. Trap B (+2): student treats the collision as perfectly inelastic (carts stick), giving common velocity p/M = 8/4 = 2 m/s. Trap D (-4): student assumes the two carts simply exchange velocities, which is only valid for equal masses, so A would take B's -4 m/s. Trap E (+8): student solves correctly but reports cart B's final velocity instead of cart A's. The figure is essential because all masses and velocities appear only there.

stem: The figure below is a snapshot (displacement versus position) of a transverse wave travelling along a long, taut string. The wave moves along the string at a constant speed of 600 m/s. Using only the information that can be read from the graph together with this speed, determine the frequency of the wave.
explanation: The horizontal axis is position, so the graph shows the wave's spatial period (its wavelength), NOT its time period. The snapshot spans 1.20 m and contains exactly 3 complete waves, so one wavelength is λ = 1.20 m ÷ 3 = 0.40 m. Applying f = v/λ = 600 m/s ÷ 0.40 m = 1500 Hz (D). The amplitude (4.0 cm) is irrelevant to frequency and is a deliberate red herring. Distractor traps: (A) 240 Hz multiplies instead of divides, computing v·λ = 600 × 0.40 — inverting the wave relation. (B) 500 Hz treats the entire 1.20 m window as a single wavelength (600 ÷ 1.20), failing to count the cycles. (C) 1000 Hz miscounts only 2 cycles in the window, giving λ = 0.60 m (600 ÷ 0.60). (E) 3000 Hz mistakes the crest-to-trough (or zero-to-zero) distance of 0.20 m for a full wavelength — i.e. uses half a wavelength (600 ÷ 0.20).

stem: The diagram shows a completed ray diagram for a thin converging lens (each grid division represents 10 cm). An upright object stands to the left of the lens, and two principal rays leaving the tip of the object cross to the right of the lens, forming a real, inverted image. Reading the object and image positions from the gridded optical axis, determine the focal length of the lens. (The focal points are NOT marked; you must use the positions shown.)
explanation: From the figure the object sits 3 divisions left of the lens, so the object distance is d_o = 30 cm; the two principal rays cross 2 divisions right of the lens, so the image distance is d_i = 20 cm. The thin-lens equation gives 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/30 + 1/20 = 2/60 + 3/60 = 5/60, so f = 12 cm (correct: B). This is consistent with the image being 2/3 the object height (m = d_i/d_o = 20/30), as the figure shows. Distractor traps: A (20 cm) reads the image distance straight off the grid and mistakes it for the focal length, assuming the image forms at the focal point — true only for a very distant object. C (25 cm) takes f as the midpoint/average of the two distances, (30+20)/2, treating focal length as halfway between object and image. D (50 cm) adds the distances, f = d_o + d_i, confusing the reciprocal sum with a direct sum. E (60 cm) uses the wrong sign convention 1/f = 1/d_o − 1/d_i = 1/30 − 1/20 = −1/60, taking the magnitude 60 cm as if the image were virtual. Each wrong option corresponds to a distinct, common misconception, and none can be reached by correctly reading both distances and applying the lens equation.

stem: In acoustics, the intensity of a sound wave is defined as the power it transports through a surface divided by the area of that surface. Working only from this definition and from the way power, energy and force are built up from mass, length and time, express the SI unit of sound intensity entirely in the base units kilogram (kg), metre (m) and second (s). Which of the following is correct?
explanation:
Build power from base units: force = mass × acceleration = kg·m·s⁻²; work/energy = force × distance = kg·m²·s⁻²; power = energy ÷ time = kg·m²·s⁻³ (the watt). Intensity = power ÷ area = (kg·m²·s⁻³) ÷ m² = kg·s⁻³, so C is correct.
A (kg·m²·s⁻³) is the unit of power itself — the trap of forgetting that intensity is power PER AREA, not power.
B (kg·s⁻²) comes from dividing energy (kg·m²·s⁻², the joule) by area instead of dividing power by area — the core energy-vs-power confusion, i.e. forgetting the extra ÷time that turns energy into power.
D (kg·m·s⁻³) results from dividing the watt by a single length m instead of an area m² — mishandling the squared dimension of area.
E (kg·m⁻¹·s⁻²) is force per area (the pascal, kg·m·s⁻² ÷ m²) — confusing intensity with pressure by starting from force rather than power.

stem: The diagram shows four monochromatic electromagnetic sources P, Q, R and S plotted on a logarithmic wavelength axis. All four emit photons that travel through vacuum at the same speed c. Using only the positions shown, which single statement is correct?
choices: S emits the highest-energy photons, and those photons also have the highest frequency.
P emits the highest-energy photons, because it has the longest wavelength of the four.
Q and R emit photons of equal energy, because they lie within the same region of the spectrum.
S has the highest frequency of the four, but therefore the lowest photon energy.
All four sources emit photons of equal energy, because every photon travels at the same speed c.
explanation: Photon energy is E = hf, and since c = fλ, frequency f = c/λ, so E ∝ 1/λ: the SMALLEST wavelength gives the highest frequency AND the highest energy. The figure is essential — only it reveals the wavelengths: P at 1 m, Q at 10⁻⁴ m, R at 10⁻⁶ m, S at 10⁻⁹ m. S has the smallest λ, so it has both the highest frequency and the highest energy, and A states exactly this consistent pair. Distractor traps: (B) is the 'long wavelength = high energy' inversion — P does have the longest wavelength (a true clause) but that gives it the LOWEST energy, so the causal claim is wrong. (C) is the 'same band ⇒ same energy' error; Q and R differ in λ by a factor of 100, so their energies differ by 100×. (D) correctly identifies S as highest frequency but decouples f from E, wrongly treating E as inversely related to f instead of E = hf. (E) is the 'equal speed ⇒ equal energy' misconception; c is the same for all EM waves and does not fix the energy, which depends on f (or λ). Only A pairs the correct quantities in the correct direction.

stem: The free-body diagram shows the three forces acting on a hanging sign: its weight and the tensions in two support cables, with each cable's angle to the horizontal marked. (Take sin 37° = cos 53° = 0.60 and cos 37° = sin 53° = 0.80.) Analysing only the forces shown in the diagram, which statement is correct?
choices: The sign is in equilibrium: the two horizontal components (96 N each) cancel, and the two vertical components (72 N + 128 N) add to exactly the 200 N weight.
The sign is NOT in equilibrium, because two forces holding an object at rest must be equal in magnitude, but here 120 N ≠ 160 N.
The sign is NOT in equilibrium, because the total upward pull of the cables is 120 N + 160 N = 280 N, which exceeds the 200 N weight.
The sign is in equilibrium purely because the cable angles are complementary (37° + 53° = 90°), which by itself guarantees balance whatever the tensions are.
The sign is NOT in equilibrium: the horizontal components cancel, but the vertical direction still has the full 200 N weight acting downward with nothing opposing it, so it accelerates down.
explanation: Equilibrium (zero acceleration) requires the vector sum of forces to be zero, i.e. BOTH component sums vanish. Resolving from the figure: horizontal — left cable 120·cos37° = 96 N (leftward), right cable 160·cos53° = 96 N (rightward): they cancel. Vertical — left 120·sin37° = 72 N up, right 160·sin53° = 128 N up, total 200 N up, balancing the 200 N weight. Both conditions hold, so A is correct. B encodes the misconception that support forces must be equal in magnitude — false, because the cables act at different angles, so unequal tensions can still balance. C adds the tension magnitudes directly as if both were vertical, ignoring that each must be resolved into components (their vertical parts are only 72 N and 128 N). D confuses necessary geometry with sufficiency: complementary angles do not by themselves guarantee balance — the magnitudes must also be correct (e.g. tensions of 120 N and 120 N at these angles would not balance). E correctly cancels the horizontal components but forgets that the SAME tensions have upward vertical components (72 N + 128 N) that oppose the weight. Only A resolves both components correctly.

stem: The tesla (T), the SI unit of magnetic flux density B, is a derived unit that can be written entirely in terms of the SI base units kilogram (kg), metre (m), second (s) and ampere (A). Starting from the magnitude of the force on a straight current-carrying wire, F = B I L, which of the following gives the correct decomposition of one tesla into base units?
explanation: Rearrange F = B I L to isolate B: B = F / (I L). The newton decomposes as F = kg·m·s⁻² (from F = ma). Substituting: B = (kg·m·s⁻²) / (A · m). The current I contributes one factor of A (base unit ampere) and the length L contributes one factor of m, which cancels the metre in the newton: B = kg·s⁻²·A⁻¹. So 1 T = kg·s⁻²·A⁻¹, option A. Trap analysis: (B) kg·m·s⁻²·A⁻¹ comes from dividing only by the current and forgetting to divide by the length L (i.e. treating F = B I) — it still carries a stray metre; this combination is in fact the newton-per-ampere, not the tesla. (C) kg·m²·s⁻²·A⁻¹ is the weber (magnetic flux Φ = B·Area), obtained by multiplying by an area instead of dividing by a length — confusing flux density with flux itself. (D) kg·s⁻²·A⁻² arises from wrongly using the force-between-two-wires relation (F ∝ I²), inserting a second factor of ampere in the denominator. (E) kg·m⁻¹·s⁻²·A⁻¹ results from dividing the newton by an area (L²) rather than a single length L, over-cancelling the metre to a negative power. Only A correctly balances base units.

stem: The figure shows every force acting on a 2 kg puck sliding on a horizontal sheet of frictionless ice, viewed from directly above (gravity acts perpendicular to the surface and is exactly balanced by the normal force, so neither is shown). Using only the forces in the diagram, what is the magnitude of the puck's acceleration?
explanation: See figure and reasoning.

stem: A dock worker drags a crate along level, horizontal ground by pulling on a rigid handle. The magnitude of the applied force, the angle the force makes with the ground, and the horizontal distance the crate travels are all given in the diagram. Using only the values shown, how much work does the applied force do on the crate over this displacement?
explanation: Work is the dot product W = F·d·cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. The displacement is horizontal, and the figure shows F = 500 N applied at 53° above the horizontal over d = 4.0 m. Only the component of the force along the motion, F·cosθ = 500·0.60 = 300 N, does work: W = 300·4.0 = 1200 J (option C). Distractor A (2000 J) ignores the angle entirely, using W = F·d = 500·4.0 — the naive 'force is parallel' error. Distractor B (1600 J) uses the sine, W = F·d·sinθ = 500·4.0·0.80, taking the vertical component (perpendicular to the motion) instead of the horizontal one; this is also the error of reading the 53° from the vertical rather than the ground. Distractor D (720 J) projects twice, W = F·d·cos²θ = 500·4.0·0.36, resolving the force AND shrinking the distance by the same factor (double counting the angle). Distractor E (0 J) over-applies the rule that a force perpendicular to displacement does no work, wrongly treating the angled pull as if it were entirely perpendicular to the ground. The angle and both magnitudes appear only in the figure, so the item cannot be answered from the text alone.

stem: The diagram shows three ideal capacitors connected across an ideal battery. Using only the values marked in the diagram, determine the total electric charge stored by the capacitor network (equal to the charge delivered by the battery), and express it in its correct SI unit.
explanation:
Reading the figure: C1 (6 μF) and C2 (3 μF) sit on the same vertical branch, so they are in SERIES, giving C1·C2/(C1+C2) = 18/9 = 2 μF. That branch is in PARALLEL with C3 (4 μF), so the network's equivalent capacitance is 2 + 4 = 6 μF. Since capacitance relates charge and voltage by C = Q/V, the charge delivered by the battery is Q = C_eq·V = (6×10⁻⁶ F)(10 V) = 6.0×10⁻⁵ C. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C), because farad × volt = (coulomb/volt) × volt = coulomb. A is correct.

Distractor traps:
B) 6.0×10⁻⁵ F — the correct numerical value but tagged with the farad, the unit of capacitance, not the coulomb. This is the exact unit-recognition error the item targets: confusing the quantity being asked for (charge) with capacitance, i.e. forgetting that in C = Q/V it is Q, not C, that is measured in coulombs.
C) 1.3×10⁻⁴ C — treats C1 and C2 as if they were in parallel, giving 6+3+4 = 13 μF and Q = 130 μC. This is the classic series/parallel topology misread of the left branch.
D) 1.3×10⁻⁵ C — treats all three capacitors as one big series string, 1/(1/6+1/3+1/4) = 1.33 μF, so Q ≈ 13 μC. Misapplies the series formula to the whole network.
E) 6.0×10⁻⁶ C — finds the correct equivalent capacitance (6 μF) but reports that number as the charge, i.e. forgets to apply Q = C·V (drops the factor of V = 10). It also silently swaps a capacitance value into coulombs.

stem: A periodic water wave, generated by a steadily vibrating paddle, travels from a deep region of a tank into a shallow region. In the deep region the wave moves at 6.0 m/s, and in the shallow region it slows to 4.0 m/s. An observer standing over the shallow region measures the distance between two adjacent wave crests to be 0.50 m. What is the frequency of the wave?
explanation:
The frequency of a wave is fixed by its source (the paddle) and does NOT change when the wave crosses into a new medium — only the speed and wavelength change. So the frequency must be computed from a matched speed–wavelength pair taken in the SAME region. The only region where wavelength is given is the shallow one: f = v/λ = 4.0 m/s ÷ 0.50 m = 8.0 Hz (A, correct).

Distractor traps:
B) 12 Hz — mismatches the media: uses the deep-region speed (6.0 m/s) with the shallow-region wavelength (6.0 ÷ 0.50). The 6.0 m/s is a deliberate lure; no deep-region wavelength is given, so it cannot legitimately be used here.
C) 10 Hz — averages the two speeds, (6.0 + 4.0)/2 = 5.0 m/s, then divides by 0.50. Reflects the misconception that a boundary quantity is the mean of the two sides.
D) 2.0 Hz — multiplies instead of divides: v × λ = 4.0 × 0.50, confusing the wave relation's structure.
E) 0.13 Hz — inverts the formula, computing the period T = λ/v = 0.50 ÷ 4.0 = 0.125 s and reporting it as if it were a frequency.

The item is selective because the correct path requires recognizing frequency invariance at a boundary (rejecting the tempting 6.0 m/s) and then applying f = v/λ to the correctly matched pair.

stem: The graph shows a snapshot of a transverse wave travelling along a stretched rope: it plots the rope's displacement against position x at one instant. A small marker attached to one point of the rope is observed to complete 45 full up-and-down oscillations in 0.90 s. Using the graph to determine the wavelength, what is the speed of the wave?
explanation: Step 1 — read the wavelength from the graph: two complete wave cycles fill the 1.0 m span shown, so one wavelength is lambda = 1.0/2 = 0.5 m. Step 2 — get the frequency from the oscillation data: f = 45 cycles / 0.90 s = 50 Hz. Step 3 — apply v = f*lambda = 50 * 0.5 = 25 m/s (C). Distractor traps: (A) 12.5 m/s takes lambda as the distance from a crest to the adjacent trough (0.25 m, a half-wavelength) — the classic 'crest-to-trough = wavelength' error — then 50*0.25. (B) 22.5 m/s reads lambda = 0.5 m correctly but uses the raw cycle count 45 as the frequency, forgetting to divide by the 0.90 s interval: 45*0.5. (D) 50 m/s reads the whole horizontal span 1.0 m as a single wavelength, ignoring that two full waves are drawn: 50*1.0. (E) 100 m/s uses the correct lambda and f but inverts the wave relation, computing f/lambda = 50/0.5 instead of f*lambda.

stem: The diagram shows a thin converging lens with optical centre O. Its focal points F and the points 2F are marked on the principal axis, and the scale beneath the axis gives every distance from the lens in centimetres. A luminous arrow-shaped object stands upright at one of the 2F points, and two principal rays (one initially parallel to the axis, one through O) have been traced through the lens to locate the image. Reading only the distances given on the diagram, determine the separation along the axis between the object and its image, and state the nature and size of the image.
choices: 48 cm; the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object
24 cm; the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object
36 cm; the image is real, inverted and half the size of the object
48 cm; the image is virtual, upright and the same size as the object
60 cm; the image is real, inverted and larger than the object
explanation: From the scale the lens-to-F distance is 12 cm, so f = 12 cm, and the object sits at 2F = 24 cm on the left. Applying 1/v = 1/f − 1/u with the object at 2f gives v = 2f = 24 cm on the opposite side; the traced rays confirm this by converging at the right-hand 2F point. Magnification m = −v/u = −1, so the image is real, inverted and the SAME size. The two distances add along the axis: 24 cm (object side) + 24 cm (image side) = 48 cm → A. Traps: B (24 cm) reports only the image distance, forgetting to add the object distance, though it correctly gets the size. C (36 cm) mistakes the 2f case for object-at-infinity behaviour, placing the image at F (v = 12, sep 24+12 = 36) and calling it diminished. D keeps the correct 48 cm but assigns the wrong nature, wrongly treating the converging lens as producing a virtual, upright image. E (60 cm) confuses the 2f case with an object between F and 2F, placing the image beyond 2F at 3f (v = 36, sep 24+36 = 60) and magnified.

stem: A narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism and separates into a spectrum. The diagram shows two of the emergent rays, P and Q, together with the undeviated direction of the original beam (dashed). The total deviation of each ray from the original direction is marked. Using the diagram, which single statement about rays P and Q is correct?
choices: Ray Q has the shorter wavelength and the higher frequency of the two.
Ray P experiences the larger refractive index inside the glass.
Ray Q travels faster than Ray P while inside the prism.
Both rays travel at the same speed inside the prism because the glass is a single medium.
Ray P has the higher frequency because it is deviated by the smaller angle.
explanation: From the figure, Ray Q is deviated more (49°) than Ray P (37°). Greater deviation means the glass presents a larger refractive index to that ray; higher n corresponds to a shorter wavelength (and therefore a higher frequency, since f = c/λ in vacuum) and a slower speed inside the glass (v = c/n). A: correct — Q bends most, so it has the largest n, the shortest wavelength, and the highest frequency. B: inverts the deviation–index relation; P bends LESS, so P has the SMALLER n, not the larger. C: assumes 'bends more / higher frequency = faster', but higher n means Q actually travels SLOWER in the glass. D: ignores dispersion — n depends on wavelength, so the two colours have different speeds even in the same glass. E: reverses the frequency relation — the less-deviated ray P has the LOWER, not higher, frequency. All four traps require mistaking which ray deviates more or misapplying one link in the deviation → n → wavelength/frequency/speed chain, and none can be settled without reading the two angles from the figure.

stem:
For all nonzero real numbers a and b, the expression

  2a − (a + b)⁻¹ · b

is equal to which of the following single fractions?
explanation:
The negative exponent applies only to (a + b), so (a + b)⁻¹ · b = b/(a + b). Then 2a − b/(a+b) = [2a(a+b) − b]/(a+b) = (2a² + 2ab − b)/(a + b), which is option A.

Distractor traps:
B (2a² − b)/(a+b): student multiplies 2a by (a+b) in the numerator but forgets the cross term, writing 2a·a = 2a² only and dropping the 2ab — an incomplete-distribution error.
C (2a − b)/(a+b): student naively places 2a over the common denominator without multiplying it by (a+b), i.e. treats 2a as if it were already 2a/(a+b) — failure to rescale the whole term.
D (2a² + 2ab − b)/b: student misreads the negative exponent as attaching to b instead of (a+b), using b⁻¹ so the common denominator becomes b — the classic "which factor does ⁻¹ bind to" misconception.
E (a + b − b)/(a+b): student treats (a+b)⁻¹·b as if it cancels to b/(a+b) but then also erroneously converts 2a into (a+b), collapsing the numerator incorrectly (also simplifies to a/(a+b), a wrong give-away form) — a spurious-cancellation trap.

stem: At the start of 2023 a research institute employed 1,500 technicians and 1,000 researchers. During 2024 the number of technicians grew by 8% and the number of researchers grew by 18%. By what percentage did the institute's total staff grow over this period?
explanation: Apply base × (1 + rate) to each group and aggregate on the true bases. Technicians: 1,500 × 1.08 = 1,620 (+120). Researchers: 1,000 × 1.18 = 1,180 (+180). Total staff goes from 2,500 to 2,800, an increase of 300, so 300 / 2,500 = 12% (B). The distractors each encode one specific error: (C) 13% averages the two rates (8% and 18%) as if the two groups were equal in size, ignoring that the larger group carries the smaller rate — the core trap. (D) 14% keeps the base-weighting but swaps the rates onto the wrong groups: (1,500 × 18% + 1,000 × 8%)/2,500 = 350/2,500. (E) 26% simply adds the two rates (8 + 18). (A) 10% subtracts the two rates (18 − 8) instead of computing the actual staff change. Because the two bases differ, the correct overall rate must lie between 8% and 18% weighted toward the larger technician base, i.e. below the 13% midpoint, which only 12% satisfies.

stem: A laboratory decade-scaler shows a numeric reading and has two buttons. The ▲ button multiplies the current reading by 10, and the ▼ button divides the current reading by 10. Starting from a reading of 0.04, a technician presses the ▲ button 5 times and the ▼ button 3 times, in some order. What is the final reading on the scaler?
explanation: Write the start as a power of ten: 0.04 = 4×10⁻². Each ▲ adds 1 to the exponent, each ▼ subtracts 1, and order does not matter. Net exponent change = +5 (five ▲) − 3 (three ▼) = +2. Final exponent = −2 + 2 = 0, so the reading is 4×10⁰ = 4 (B). Distractor A (0.0004) reverses the two buttons — treating ▲ as divide and ▼ as multiply gives −2 − 5 + 3 = −4, i.e. 4×10⁻⁴. Distractor C (40) comes from misreading the place value of 0.04 as 4×10⁻¹, giving −1 + 5 − 3 = +1. Distractor D (4000) ignores the ▼ presses entirely and applies only 0.04 × 10⁵. Distractor E (4,000,000) treats ▼ as if it also shifted the value up (both buttons adding zeros): −2 + 5 + 3 = +6, i.e. 4×10⁶. Only the net shift of +2 applied to the correct −2 starting exponent yields a whole-number reading of 4.

stem: A fire-detection unit contains two sensors that operate independently. When smoke is present, sensor 1 triggers with probability 3/5 and sensor 2 triggers with probability 5/8. The unit raises the alarm whenever at least one of its two sensors triggers. If smoke is present, the probability that the unit raises the alarm is:
explanation: "At least one" is handled through its complement: P(alarm) = 1 - P(neither sensor triggers). Because the sensors are independent, P(neither) = (1 - 3/5)(1 - 5/8) = (2/5)(3/8) = 6/40 = 3/20. So P(alarm) = 1 - 3/20 = 17/20 = 0.85, which lies between 3/4 (0.75) and 9/10 (0.90) → D. Distractor traps: A (< 1/5) reports the complement 3/20 = 0.15 itself, i.e. the "neither triggers" probability, forgetting the final subtraction. B (between 1/3 and 1/2) comes from misreading "at least one" as "both," giving (3/5)(5/8) = 3/8 = 0.375. C (between 1/2 and 3/4) is either the average of the two probabilities (3/5 + 5/8)/2 ≈ 0.61, or 1 - P(both) = 1 - 3/8 = 5/8 = 0.625, wrongly treating the alarm event as "not both." E (> 9/10) results from simply adding the independent probabilities, 3/5 + 5/8 = 1.225, failing to remove the overlap and treating that inflated value as a high probability. Only the correct complement-of-the-intersection path yields 0.85, band D.

stem: The solid curve in the figure is the graph of the parabola y = x² − 2x − 2. Five points, labelled A through E, are marked on the integer grid; several of them lie visually close to the parabola, so their position cannot be settled by eye. Read each point's coordinates from the grid and use the equation to decide which single marked point actually lies ON the parabola (i.e. exactly satisfies y = x² − 2x − 2).
explanation:
Read the coordinates off the grid: A(−1,−1), B(2,0), C(3,1), D(1,−1), E(0,−3). A point lies on the curve only if its y-value equals x²−2x−2.

Correct — C(3,1): 3²−2(3)−2 = 9−6−2 = 1, which matches the point's y-coordinate, so C is exactly on the parabola.

Distractor traps (each a distinct error):
• A(−1,−1): true value is (−1)²−2(−1)−2 = 1+2−2 = 1, so the curve passes through (−1,1), not (−1,−1). This point is the landing spot for a student who squares the negative x incorrectly, treating (−1)² as −1 to get −1+2−2 = −1.
• B(2,0): true value is 4−4−2 = −2, so the curve is at (2,−2). B(2,0) is where a student lands after dropping the constant term, computing only 4−4 = 0.
• D(1,−1): true value is 1−2−2 = −3 (this is the vertex). D(1,−1) is the point obtained by dropping the linear −2x term: 1−2 = −1.
• E(0,−3): true value is the y-intercept 0−0−2 = −2, so the curve is at (0,−2). E(0,−3) sits one unit lower — the trap of assigning the vertex's minimum height (−3) to the y-axis, confusing the lowest point of the graph with the intercept.

Because the four wrong points each sit only about one grid unit off the curve, they cannot be eliminated visually; exact substitution of the grid-read coordinates is required.

stem: Two regular polygons, labelled P and Q, are each inscribed in a circle, as shown in the figure. In each diagram, radii have been drawn to every vertex, dividing the polygon into congruent triangular sectors, and the apothem a (the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side) is marked. Using only the information in the figure, decide which single statement is correct.
choices: Q has the greater total area, yet each of its triangular sectors has a smaller area than each triangular sector of P.
P has the greater total area, because its individual triangular sectors are each larger than those of Q.
The two polygons have equal total area, since they are inscribed in circles of equal radius.
Q has the greater total area, and its apothem a is shorter than the apothem of P.
Q has the greater total area, and each of its triangular sectors has a larger area than each triangular sector of P.
explanation: From the figure, P is a regular hexagon (6 sides) and Q a regular octagon (8 sides), inscribed in circles of the SAME radius R. Each polygon splits into n congruent triangles with apex angle 360°/n at the centre, so one sector has area ½R²·sin(360°/n) and the whole polygon has area n·½R²·sin(360°/n). Hexagon: 6·½R²·sin60° ≈ 2.598R². Octagon: 8·½R²·sin45° ≈ 2.828R². So Q (more sides) has the greater total area, approaching the circle's πR² ≈ 3.142R² — the monotonicity being tested. But per sector, sin45° < sin60°, so each octagon triangle (≈0.354R²) is SMALLER than each hexagon triangle (≈0.433R²): Q wins on area only because it has more, smaller pieces. That compound truth is A. Trap B inverts the whole relationship — it assumes larger individual pieces must give a larger total, ignoring the piece count (fewer big triangles lose to more small ones). Trap C is the headline misconception the competency targets: equal radius does NOT give equal area; only side count decides. Traps D and E are the discriminators — both correctly state Q has the greater area (so 'Q is bigger' alone cannot settle the item), but each attaches a false second clause: D claims Q's apothem is shorter, whereas apothem = R·cos(180°/n) grows with n (octagon 0.924R > hexagon 0.866R, moving toward R); E claims Q's sectors are individually larger, the exact opposite of the sin(360°/n) result. Only A pairs the correct area comparison with the correct per-sector comparison, and every clause requires reading the side counts and equal radii from the figure.

stem: In digital image processing a "gamma" transform sends a normalized pixel brightness x (with 0 < x < 1) to the value x^γ. The figure below shows the identity line y = x (dashed) together with two gamma curves, labelled ① and ②, corresponding to the exponents γ = 1/3 and γ = 3 in an unspecified order. Reading the graph, which statement is correct?
choices: ① is y = x^(1/3) and ② is y = x^3; throughout 0 < x < 1 one has x^(1/3) > x > x^3.
